subtopic: REPORTED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
It
seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this is a matter of urgent public importance and that there is every reason for Your Honour to allow the debate which has been proposed by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition.
I think this matter is urgent on three grounds. I think it is urgent, in the first place, because a statement ought to be made in the house today by the minister responsible for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in order to allay the fears and misunderstanding which are prevalent throughout the country with regard to the recent dismissal of the two co-hosts of the program "This Hour Has Seven Days".
The motion moved by the Leader of the Opposition contains a statement made by the Secretary of State to the effect that the dispute over the program "This Hour Has Seven Days" is only symptomatic of a much wider discord within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. It seems to me most urgent that the House of Commons and the country should know what is the state of affairs within that organization. Certainly the statement made yesterday by Mr. Ouimet has done nothing to allay those fears. There is a contradiction contained in that statement. The chairman alluded to the fact that the producer of the program had mishandled controversial questions, but at the same time said that Mr. Leiterman, who is the producer, would continue with the program next season.
We have, therefore, the man who is responsible being retained on the program and the two co-hosts being removed from the program. This certainly indicates some breakdown in responsibility, and indicates that the

reasons which have been given for the dismissals are not the true reasons at all. The minister's statement, therefore, that there is a crisis boiling up within the C.B.C. would seem to be warranted. I think this house and the country have a right to know what is the situation.
The second ground for urgency is that there ought to be a debate in this house so the government can hear the views of the members regarding this whole question and refer it to the standing committee on broadcasting. Statements which have been made by those within the corporation, statements which have been made by those outside the corporation, and statements which have been made by Mr. Robert Fowler, who was the royal commissioner looking into this matter, all ought to be referred to the standing committee. I am told Mr. Fowler was to be interviewed on the program "This Hour Has Seven Days", and that this interview was quashed by the management. If this is true this matter ought to be settled, and ought to be settled immediately, by having this whole question referred to a committee.
The third and most important reason for urgency, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that there is a grave possibility of either mass resignations by producers and performers or a strike by some of those in important positions within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Either of these propositions would do great harm to our national, publicly owned broadcasting system. All of us who believe in a national, publicly owned broadcasting system would be loath to see such a thing happen. If it could be prevented by having some arbitration machinery set up immediately to go into this question and prevent the loss of some very important and very capable staff, I think that should be acted upon immediately. I think it would be unwise for this house to sit here and allow the situation within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to deteriorate further. This is a most urgent matter which ought to be discussed, and it should be discussed today.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. J. Mcllraiih (Minister of Public Works):
speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: REPORTED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the sole question before Your Honour for decision at the moment, as I see it, is the matter of urgency of debate. The hon. member who has just taken his seat indicated that there was certain information he wanted the house to have. The house has already taken action in the matter by referring the estimates relating to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the standing
April 19. 1966

committee on broadcasting on March 22, and I understand those estimates are now before that committee.
I know of no better way of obtaining the information which the hon. member asserts would be the proper concern of this house than by having the appropriate witnesses examined before that committee. There is no reason why that cannot be done today. If the hon. member wishes it to be done today, then that is a matter for the committee.
I do not know whether the hon. member has taken the usual steps to have that done, but the point I wish to make clear, Mr. Speaker, is this. You have been asked to set aside the ordinary business of the house for today, business which is also quite important, in order to permit debate of this matter in this house without hearing witnesses and without having available the information which the hon. member indicated was so important.
I suggest that his whole argument has indicated that the correct method to discuss this matter is through the committee which has been constituted and which has the matter before it. There is no reason to move a motion to withdraw the matter from the committee at this time. In other words, no case has been made for urgency of debate within the meaning of standing order 26.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPORTED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the urgency of this matter is concerned I am quite surprised at the attitude taken by the minister on behalf of the government. I do not think there has ever been a matter which in so short a time has brought about so much antagonism in all parts of Canada. Indeed, I understand that some 3,800 or more telegrams have been received by the C.B.C. in this connection. I personally have received a greater number than in respect of any other matter in the last couple of years. The question of urgency is apparent in view of an aroused public opinion and the need for parliament to look into this matter.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam made mention of the reaction among C.B.C. employees in consequence of what they believe to have been arbitrary treatment on the part of management. He also mentioned the Fowler commission and the recommendations of that commission. My information, in view of those recommendations, is that because two officials connected with the "Seven Days" program, one in Ottawa and one in Toronto, gave their views to the Fowler commission,
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation these two gentlemen have been advised that their contracts are to be terminated because they have not left a good image of the C.B.C. or in any event that there are doubts about the statements they made before the Fowler commission on broadcasting, and therefore they have lost their right to be treated in the manner in which one would expect.
There cannot be anything more urgent than this. This is not a matter which can be shelved away, as I see it, by saying that some other institution or body can look after it. This is a matter concerning a great national body that incidentally was set up under a Conservative government, under Mr. Bennett. I want to make that clear. That body was to be an institution for the benefit of the Canadian people, not for the glorification of those in high positions.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
The Canadian people contribute fabulous amounts of money to the corporation, through parliament. We have a right to expect that those sums shall be expended in a way that is in keeping with the responsibilities of that corporation.
I therefore say there is urgency, and I am amazed at the attitude of the government house leader in this regard. If the members of the government do not know there is urgency, then they have not opened their telegrams.

subtopic: REPORTED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of the Leader of the Opposition suggesting it is urgent to discuss the action taken by the C.B.C. with regard to the program "This Hour Has Seven Days", hosted by Messrs. Patrick Watson and Laurier LaPierre, does not seem to me as urgent as the Leader of the Opposition would have us believe. I feel there are at present in Canada much more urgent matters than to determine whether the program "This Hour Has Seven Days" should continue to be hosted by Messrs. Watson and LaPierre.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, I know personally Messrs. Watson and LaPierre. I admire a great deal those two Canadians who have performed a tremendous job at the C.B.C. in order to present the program "This Hour Has Seven Days" to the Canadian people.
We in parliament should keep in mind that, in the past, the hosts of many programs have changed in practically similar circumstances, and neither the Leader of the Opposition nor
April 19, 1966

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation anyone else objected because the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was under a commission independent of parliament. In fact, the C.B.C. was not interfered with.
Mr. Speaker, there will always be an opportunity to discuss the Watson-LaPierre case, and others, before the committee on broadcasting, films and assistance to the arts, where all members are invited. When the estimates of the Department of the Secretary of State are before us we can bring up this question of the program "This Hour Has Seven Days" and establish the facts concerning Messrs. Watson and LaPierre.
Now, even if we were to discuss this matter today I do not think we could reach an immediate agreement. As I said a while ago, Mr. Speaker, I feel there are far more pressing things to be attended to.
During the last electoral campaign the government promised to wage war on poverty in Canada. That is a far more important matter than the situation in which Messrs. Watson and LaPierre find themselves at the present time. That is something far more urgent than the program "This Hour Has Seven Days".
Everybody appreciated the program, granted, but there are legislative measures to be introduced and studied here, in Ottawa, which are of far greater importance. And, at any rate, as I have already said, "This Hour Has Seven Days" can always be discussed when the estimates of the Secretary of State come up, or else before the appropriate committee.
Now, for my part, I do not believe in the need of adjourning the house to consider that specific case. The Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) stated that the row over that program is symptomatic of more fundamental problems within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and that the attention paid to it is an indication that there is serious trouble within the C.B.C. Everybody is convinced of that, even the Leader of the Opposition when he was Prime Minister of Canada. In fact, at that time he did nothing to correct what took place under his own administration.
Mr. Speaker, I fully agree with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith) that there is not so much urgency to debate this case, but that, on the other hand, there are much more capital issues to be discussed today, in the Ottawa Parliament, for the well-being of the population. The firing of two individuals because of political pressures

or other intrigues not specified in the newspapers is secondary.
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the urgency is somewhere else than within the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation today.

subtopic: REPORTED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
I think the very unusual statement which was made a few days ago by the Secretary of State, to the effect that there was far more difficulty and trouble brewing within the C.B.C. than had been apparent up to that time, is one with which this house should be concerned. However, I believe we have set up the proper method of dealing with this kind of information inasmuch as the committee on broadcasting now has the authority to go into this matter at once should it choose to do so. After all, the standing committees of this house are in effect an extension of the house itself.
I think, Mr. Speaker, you will also have to consider this motion to adjourn the house under standing order No. 26 in the light of paragraph 1 of citation No. 100 in Beau-chesne's fourth edition, which states that a motion to adjourn the house under standing order No. 26 must involve the administrative responsibility of the government. The motion before us deals specifically with a question of programming by the C.B.C., and over the years there has been great resistance on the part of the government, and in particular on the part of the minister reporting for the corporation, to any attempt by members of this house to become involved in C.B.C. programming.
This is true of previous governments as well as of the government now in office. I can recall ministers who have held responsibility in the past for reporting to this house on C.B.C. affairs adamantly refusing to accept the kind of criticism which involved C.B.C. programming. Time after time they claimed it was not the responsibility of the minister reporting to parliament to become involved in the programming of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. For these reasons I think it would be difficult to accept a motion such as is now before us, a motion which involves programming, when over the years all governments have claimed they do not have an administrative responsibility in this area.
Another point is this. Urgency of debate requires that the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the house do not permit the subject to be brought up early enough,
April 19. 1966	COMMONS
with the result that the public interest suffers. I suggest that today, or almost immediately now that the estimates have been referred to the standing committees, the particular committee concerned, which as I have said is an extension of this house, can inquire into this matter.
[DOT] (3:00 p.m.)
In my view this would be a far more useful exercise than conducting a debate on the floor of the house. The committee has power to call officials of the C.B.C. if it so wishes in order to find out what is at the bottom of this trouble which the Secretary of State claims is brewing within the corporation. We could call in the president and ask him if there has been gross insubordination sufficient to cause him to dismiss these men for the ensuing season. Until we get the rest of this information I do not think a debate on the floor of the house could serve any useful purpose.
I think what has happened during the course of the last two or three days is something that could have been avoided if the broadcasting committee had been set up several months ago, but it is too late to complain about that now. I sincerely believe the time could be spent far more usefully in calling the C.B.C. officials before the committee and finding out what is at the bottom of all this discord within the C.B.C. That would be far more useful than having a debate here without knowing what the president and other administrators have on their minds.
I also suggest that if the Secretary of State is aware of a lot of difficulty within the C.B.C. administration she should make a statement to the house about it. This she has not done, but she could make such a statement to the broadcasting committee. After all, we in this house do provide the funds for the C.B.C., and if it is not functioning well and properly and in the interests of the Canadian public generally, and she knows about it then she has a responsibility to tell the broadcasting committee or the House of Commons.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I refer you to the first paragraph of citation 100, which says the matter for debate must involve the administrative responsibility of the government and, if we are to follow the pattern of the past, we have to accept that C.B.C. programming is not a responsibility of the government.

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation regret I cannot agree with the hon. member for Villeneuve and the hon. member for Medicine Hat in the emphasis they have placed on the question of programming as mentioned in the motion presented by the Leader of the Opposition. Programming is only a part of the whole problem, and if a careful reading is made of the motion it will be seen it deals with a crisis of uncertainty in broadcasting, particularly in the C.B.C.
On the question of urgency I point out that within the rules of the house the debate which we are to continue today is on fiscal matters, and must run for another four or five days or until the end of this week. Certainly I find it rather passing strange that the hon. member for Medicine Hat would cite a reference in Beauchesne with regard to the administrative responsibility of the government. By statute the C.B.C. is responsible to parliament, and parliament is in this house. It is to parliament that the C.B.C. is responsible. Therefore it is quite right that this matter should be discussed here if it is one of urgency. I suggest that the hon. member for Medicine Hat is placing the cart before the horse in that he is subordinating parliamentary to government responsibility.
The third point I would like to make is with regard to the broadcasting committee. A decision by the majority of that committee to relegate this matter to some indefinite date is not appealable to the house. It is not even referable to the house. What has been referred to that committee are the estimates of the corporation. If in deciding its agenda the committee puts this matter off to some indeterminate date and the Secretary of State does not appear before parliament to repeat the rather grave statement which she made at a partisan political meeting, then this house is stultified.
I suggest to Your Honour that now is the time for the minister to come forward to make her statement, to elaborate on it, and to give us the reasons why she made it originally. That is the crisis of uncertainty with regard to the C.B.C. The question of one program or another matters not. After all, one has only to go back to the records of June, 1959 to see that some hon. ministers now sitting opposite put forward a similar
April 19, 1966

Canadian Broadcasting Corporation type of motion to discuss an internal C.B.C. matter concerning a less popular radio program. I suggest they cannot now argue on both sides of the question and I put it to Your Honour that this motion is entertaina-ble. It is urgent as to debate. subtopic: REPORTED CRISIS-MOTION FOR ADJOURNMENT UNDER STANDING ORDER 26
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to urge you to accept the motion on the following grounds. First, I think it is a great error, whether deliberate or innocent, to interpret the motion as one dealing only with programming in the C.B.C. What the motion seeks is a debate on the crisis of uncertainty and chaos in the affairs of the C.B.C. There is the reported admission by the Secretary of State that the row over "Seven Days" is an iceberg symptomatic of more fundamental matters within the corporation, and there is her acknowledgement that there is serious trouble within the corporation.
I submit that the motion seeks to have a debate on the serious trouble and controversy within the corporation, a corporation which is responsible to parliament through the minister. It is wrong to suggest that the motion and members supporting it are concerned with details of programming. We in this group are as anxious as other hon. members to leave the C.B.C. free to deal with its own programming arrangements.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Medicine Hat was right when he said it is important that the minister should make a statement to the house. This is precisely what the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam suggested was one of the reasons of urgency for the motion, because it would enable the minister to make her statement today, at a time when everybody in Canada and all members of this house are concerned about the problem.
Third, Mr. Speaker, for obvious reasons I have not had as much experience as many other hon. members in these matters but I recall looking up a number of occasions when subjects were debated under standing order 26 and, speaking from memory but I think accurately, the debates ended in the subject matter being referred to some committee or other. The fact that there is a debate on a matter of urgent public importance does not preclude the matter going to a committee. On the contrary, that may be the desired end. Therefore the suggestion that this matter be referred to a standing committee, and other 
similar suggestions, could be implemented after debate in the house today.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that what was said by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and the Leader of the Opposition as to urgency is obvious and compelling, namely that all the reports indicate that unless there is some assurance given through a discussion on the floor of this house we may have wholesale resignations from the C.B.C., or a strike by producers or some other group within the C.B.C. It will not do any good at all to have the standing committee on broadcasting consider this matter either a day or two days from now, if, in the meantime, irreparable harm has been done in the corporation by action which seems to be contemplated by responsible staff members of the corporation.
For these reasons I urge you to accept the motion as presented.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)

speechtext:
Order, please, The Chair has heard arguments for and against the motion proposed by the right hon. leader of the official opposition. While I do not wish to prevent further discussion, I believe the Chair has been sufficiently enlightened in respect of this matter to reach a decision.
As hon. members well know, the guiding principles in matters of this kind are to be found in Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 100. The hon. member for Medicine Hat referred the Chair particularly to paragraph 1 of that citation. However, I prefer to base my ruling on paragraph 3 of citation 100 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, which reads as follows:
'Urgency' within this rule does not apply to the matter itself, but it means 'urgency of debate', when the ordinary opportunities provided by the rules of the House do not permit the subject to be brought on early enough and public interest demands that discussion take place immediately.
In referring to the question of urgency of debate the hon. member for Edmonton West drew attention to the fact that the immediate business of this house was the continuation of the budget debate, and that there could be no discussion of this matter during the next four or five days. I agree with the hon. member to this extent. This matter cannot be discussed while there is a motion of non-confidence before the house, and while there are before us an amendment and a sub-amendment, both dealing with financial matters. Any attempt to discuss the subject matter of the motion now before the house would be out of
April 19. 1966

order, because of irrelevancy, during our consideration of those two want of confidence motions.
I should point out that the subamendment now before us will be disposed of this evening, and that the amendment will be disposed of on Thursday evening. Assuming that the government survives both amendments there will then be an opportunity to discuss the subject matter of the proposed motion when we have before us the simple motion that the Speaker do now leave the chair. It seems to me that will provide an early enough opportunity to discuss this matter.
In view of these facts I cannot accept the motion proposed by the right hon. leader of the official opposition.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, April 1, consideration of the motion of Hon. Mitchell

The Budget-Mr. Walker Sharp (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Monteith, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).

speakeroldname: Mr. J. E. Walker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I was interrupted by the clock when the budget debate was adjourned prior to Easter there was only time for me to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) on his excellent non-partisan presentation and to point out that the sense of control, firmness and knowledgeable management that emanated from his speech was welcomed by all sections of the country. Since then, on the street interviews, as carried in the daily press, confirm the feeling of confidence on the part of the average citizen in this budget and in the various measures for controlled development of Canada that were put forward.
I trust it is in order to mention that my own minister, the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Benson), undoubtedly made his usual wise and experienced counsel available to the Minister of Finance, and it is only right that his contribution should be noted here. Being a very modest and humble man it would never enter his head to seek this kind of recognition for himself, but I believe I can expose him to flattering remarks at this time. At any rate, it is good to be on the side of the angels.
This business of making a budget and of its presentation is something that has intrigued me for a long time. I wonder whether the importance of budget night is not becoming magnified out of proportion. I am not speaking of the importance of a budget itself. I am speaking of the custom that has grown up where by budget night becomes the surprise package focal point of our hopes and plans, our disappointments or satisfactions, our approval or condemnation of a whole year's program. There is a sort of Christmas morning gift giving or taking atmosphere about the whole thing that seems to me to be a little artificial and in many cases clouds the basic reasoning and logic behind a budget. Many press stories simplify the whole thing into two easily read lists. One is entitled "These things will cost you more" and the other, "These things will cost you less."
There are some well-researched articles on a budget and its implications in the financial
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Walker pages and editorially but generally my impression is that the main interest on the front pages seems to be focused on whether taxes have gone up or down. Indeed, this concentration on the single point of higher or lower taxes leads many political columnists and pundits to forecast whether general elections are imminent. This is too cynical an approach for me, and I believe the importance of a budget is obscured by these observations.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I think the Canadian people are politically mature enough to understand why taxes go up or down. I think they are more vitally interested in great, imaginative national programs of resources development, medical and scientific research, educational opportunities and external aid than they are in the cost of a package of cigarettes or a bottle of liquor or a few dollars more in income tax. If this budget-making process could be levelled out over the year without this aura of "Guess what's in it for me", and "Do not open before budget night", I think a government's forward planning and management techniques could be more easily applied to five- and ten-year projects. Some of this is done now by individual pieces of legislation. The Canada-United States auto agreement is a case in point. I should like to see our citizens made aware of where their money is going and why it is going there and not just how much they are asked to pay. I believe their sense of involvement and participation in the nation's development and destiny would be heightened.
I know there are some budgetary matters that because of their effect on the stock and bond markets must be highly secret until the "big night". But in many other matters I see no harm-indeed, would it not be beneficial- in having the widest possible open discussion on plans, projects and measures for some months preceding the budget. This would do away with sudden jolts or the delaying of business decisions and an artificial slow-down of development on the part of industry and others who feel they must wait and see what the budget says.
If we used our budgets as a weapon for the achievement of say a four- or five-year development goal and that goal was thoroughly understood by every segment of Canadian society, would this not make the Speech from the Throne much more authoritative? Budget time provides a field day for politicians. Parliament is in the limelight and all of us, the professional experts and the amateurs-I

am in the latter category as hon. members have rightly assumed by now-get the opportunity to speak to the nation. We tell the people in unmistakable political overtones what the budget means. But the people feel left out. I want them involved mentally and not just financially.
I know that a budget controls by acceleration or deceleration the rate of growth of our country. But it does this in accordance with conditions that exist or threaten to exist on a short term basis. Can we have a closer alliance between this budgetary control and our economic and physical five- and ten-year development goals? Are there not other ways of taking the heat out of a fast running economic motor than by lightening the load for a short time? Are we trying to get too much milk from too few cows? When this happens you can do one of three things: carry on and ruin the cow, cut back on her milk production, or get more cows.
If our present manpower resources are numerically inadequate to reach the full potentialities of growth for Canada, I would suppose we should increase those manpower resources quickly rather than lowering our aim. I have felt for a long time now that immigration on whatever scale is necessary to meet our development objectives should be considered as an economic resource as well as cultural and human resource.
There are great differences of opinion in this area. I do not propose to go into it further at this time other than to mention two opposing views on the same front page of the Financial Post of April 2, 1966. The heading of the first article reads: "Do We Really Have A Skills Shortage? Experts suspicious." I quote:
Supplying the facts on skillpower will be the role of an important branch being set up inside the new federal manpower department. It is charged with going into the field to gather employment data, then processing it into detailed and useful forms which can be used in measuring Canada's manpower needs and resources.
This is the result of a growing suspicion among government manpower planners that the skill shortage in Canada may not be nearly as acute as it appears. "There are so few facts to work on," a senior Ottawa official explains. "There are assumptions based on isolated examples, but we lack any really effective and sophisticated system for measuring our manpower resources. We are even worse off when it comes down to measuring manpower utilization."
April 19, 1966

The other front page article is headed, "Men Are Available To Do It Now", and reads:
From Ottawa earlier this week also came news of a long overdue change in this country's approach to skillpower problems. The embryo Department of Manpower will henceforth find out from industry as precisely as it can what skilled manpower needs will be in the months ahead and translate these into training and immigration policies.
This goes far to solve a paradox for policymakers brought about by the steady step-up of the Canadian economy toward capacity operation.
On the one hand we have evidence of an economy hamstrung by shortages of skills. Aircraft orders turned down for want of appropriate workers. Order backlogs one-third higher than a year ago in the plants of industrial machinery producers. Companies and provinces sending abroad for skilled hands for work ranging from textiles to mining. At the same time there have been equally disturbing indications that some so-called shortages are more talk than reality.
Who is right? I think it is time we found out. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and his government, the Liberal government I am proud to support, must be praised for setting up the machine for the establishment of this new ministry under the guidance of a courageous and dedicated Canadian-he has just left the house-who has quietly won the respect and affection of his caucus colleagues and of the house as well, I believe. I refer to the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Marchand).
If any hon. members think, Mr. Speaker, because I have so far spent little time in praising certain budget items, that I am quietly criticizing the budget, they are away off base. For its timing and in the context of traditional budget procedures since our earliest parliaments, this budget is one of the better ones. I will certainly be voting to sustain the good judgment of the finance minister and of the government when the division bells ring, as I hope will all members of the house.
In the time remaining, Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of this house and I hope to the attention of all patriotic Canadians east and west an issue of immediate paramount importance. At least, I conceive it to be so and I do not stand alone in my concern. This matter does not directly concern itself with the budget but its relationship thereto is apparent. Frankly, I am convinced that it is of more immediate and lasting consequence to every Canadian man, woman and child than the budget itself. The issue I bring before the house, Mr. Speaker, is the whole question of the extent of foreign
The Budget-Mr. Walker ownership and control of Canadian resources and industry in 1966, one year before the celebration of our hundredth birthday. Are we quietly strolling down the road to national oblivion? Is there an inherently dangerous relationship between massive foreign ownership and economic and then political sovereignty.
I spoke earlier, Mr. Speaker, of the desirability of communication and public discussion of national goals and projects. If ever a question of the greatest public concern cried out for the broadest public discussion right now it is this one. I should like to see the Canadian people committed one way or the other by the time of our one hundredth anniversary a little over a year from now. What will we be saying as a nation on July 1, 1967-"We wonder what is going to happen to us by 2,000 A.D." or "We know what we will make of Canada by 2,000 A.D?"
I believe this is the major issue of the day. Really it is the only issue because, until it is faced and settled for generations to come, discussions of other matters, including budgets, are academic. We may be spending money for nothing. The moment of truth has arrived for us as a nation and as individual Canadians.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
The conscious settlement and decision of this issue in our heads and hearts could prove to be our salvation as a united country. It could lift us out of our introspection and destructive self-criticism, this pulling up the flower to see if the roots are growing. I am convinced that the spiritual resources of most Canadians in every province are more than equal to the challenge and responsibility of owning Canada. This is a big enough challenge to stir their loyalty; this is a great enough goal to enlist their devotion. It is tough enough to use all their muscles and energy and creativeness; it could be the moral equivalent of war for a peace-loving people. There is a contented peacefulness that comes with the tranquility of the grave and there is the peace and poise of a people embarked on a great adventure. I believe I know what kind Canadians will choose when the issue is put to them.
The first question to decide is whether economic and political domination follow large foreign equity ownership of a country's economy. Where is the danger point? The second question is: In this interdependent world how do we handle this problem without becoming selfish national isolationists,
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Walker without giving ideological comfort to the enemies of freedom and individual liberty, without making enemies of traditional friends and allies whose friendship is valued and unquestioned?
Our aim should be clear: under our own ownership and control to make the greatest contribution our talents allow to the awakening of the sleeping Canadian giant and then, in full co-operation with all nations, to work for equality of opportunity and justice through the rule of law for all human beings, black, yellow or white.
There are those, Mr. Speaker, who believe that Canada can accomplish these aims by becoming economically integrated in the North American complex. By submerging or erasing borders we become part of a larger unit. This thinking, which is represented on both sides of the 49th parallel, has come to be known as continentalism. Those who see more good than evil in foreign ownership penetration into Canada's economy have been called continentalists. For want of a better word those who take the opposite view have been called nationalists-economic nationalists or political nationalists. I prefer the word "Canadians."
Fundamentally-and I hope I am not simplifying this too much-a continentalist seems to think, consciously or otherwise, that whatever is good for North America is good for Canada. He sees no direct relationship between national self-determination, economically, politically or culturally, and the eventual total integration of Canadian and United States economies. If figures mean anything, then the present rate of takeover of Canadian resources, business and industry can lead only to that end. If there is no danger to Canadian nationhood in such an intertwining, we are very fortunate people. However, if there are unknown contingent liabilities involved in such an arrangement which affect all living Canadians and those yet to come, then we are embarked on a hazardous adventure. Those who have done any thinking at all about Canada's future must surely ask themselves; What are we getting into?
It is time, Mr. Speaker, for the fullest and widest public discussion from coast to coast about this whole matter. I ask my generation to answer these questions: Are we giving away our past which we did not earn, and our future which does not belong to us? As temporary custodians of this entity called Canada, have we the right to sell the family assets without reference to our heirs?


If we Canadians can have the best of both worlds, economic and political control of our country plus unprecedented prosperity through foreign equity investment, then everything is coming up roses. I do not believe we can. The hard cold fact of financial equity investment is that political power is always used eventually to protect that investment. We are naive to think otherwise. All the weeping and wailing and gnashing of teeth will be to no avail if we wake up some morning and find we have lost the right to make our economic and political decisions for all time. And we will have no one to blame but ourselves-not the Americans, not the Japanese, not the Germans, just ourselves. It makes much more sense to me to ask individual nationals of other countries to come here and help us develop our nation from within as Canadians then to import dollars and have them develop and control it from without as non-Canadians.
In terms of labels it is already clear I am an economic nationalist. I believe that whatever is good for Canada is good for North America and the world. I want Canada to be able to speak forever with all the power and freedom of a nation in full control of its future. This does not preclude collaboration and the fullest co-operation with other nations whose aims are compatible with ours. It does mean that we are under economic obligation to no one to compromise our convictions or destroy our destiny. Who is going to develop and own Canada? Other people or Canadians?
This is far too broad a subject to cover in one short speech. If I have done nothing more today than to put question marks in people's minds, to start them seriously thinking and talking about this subject, I am satisfied. No government by itself can solve this question; it is up to the Canadian people. They must make the decision or, shall I say, twenty million individual decisions. To do this they must have the facts. There must be discussion and debate. Either this issue is the most important one, the important one, facing Canadians today or it is of no consequence. Either these figures from the Financial Post of November 3, 1962 are vitally important or they are harmless statistics.
I ask hon. members to note the percentage of foreign equity ownership in the following industries in Canada. This is in the manufacturing area and these are 1959 figures: Rubber, 90 per cent; pulp and paper, 38 per cent;
April 19, 1966
agricultural machinery, 55 per cent; automobiles and parts, 96 per cent; electrical apparatus, 67 per cent; chemicals, 52 per cent; total manufacturing, 44 per cent; petroleum and natural gas, 69 per cent; mining, 53 per cent. Either these figures are vitally important or they are harmless statistics.
Either the following remarks by Beland Honderich of the Toronto Star are terribly important or they are just fillers for an after dinner speech. These are excerpts from the address given by Mr. Honderich on March 12, 1965, to the United States and Canadian members of the International Press Institute in Quebec city:
Total foreign investment in 1961 was just under $24 billion and increasing rapidly. Figures have not been published since 1961 but today it is probably in excess of $25 billion.
To express it another way, if the volume of foreign investment in the United States was as great as it is in Canada, it would total over $375 billion. And that, gentlemen, is considerably more than the combined assets of the 500 largest corporations in the United States.
Foreigners control one out of every three companies with assets of more than $1 million. They control two out of every three firms worth $25 million or more. No other developed country in the world has so many key industries under foreign control. If the same situation existed in the United States, General Motors, Ford, Chrysler, General Electric, Westinghouse, U.S. Rubber, Goodyear, I.B.M. and literally hundreds of the largest companies would be controlled by foreigners.
I continue to quote from this address by Mr. Honderich.
Foreign investment which brings with it new technical knowhow for the development of Canadian resources, and provides new jobs for Canadians, obviously contributes to the national good. But even in these cases there should be provision for Canadian participation in ownership. Canadians have a right, I submit, to share in the prosperity of Canadian business.
Foreign capital, on the other hand, that does not add to our productive facilities and, instead, merely brings about a change of ownership of an existing plant, should be subject to close scrutiny.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I polled my electors a few months ago on this problem and had over 2,700 replies. The figures are enlightening. My question was in four parts:
Are you aware of the extent of foreign ownership of "Canadian" industries and national resources?
The answer was yes, 88 per cent.
Are you concerned about this?
The answer was yes, 63 per cent.
Should steps be taken to reverse this trend?
The Budget-Mr. T. M. Bell
Yes, 61 per cent.
If necessary, would you accept a temporary lower standard of living to accomplish this?
Yes, 40 per cent; only 40 per cent, closer to one-third than one-half.
Now you see why I say that it is up to Canadians to make this corporate decision. It is their country. It is their children's country. It is their devotion and commitment to Canada's second century that is on trial. I believe the danger flags are flying. The time has come to face the facts to make a national decision one way or the other. We are all involved. No one can escape this obligation to decide on Canada's future.
Let us move quickly with the Canada Development Corporation. Let us ask the Economic Council of Canada to move quickly on clause (d) of section 9 of the act which spells out a particular duty "to study means of increasing Canadian participation in the ownership, control and management of industries in Canada." Let us get all the experienced counsel available and determine whether we are travelling on a safe high-road to prosperity and power or in a borrowed vehicle down a dead-end street.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to follow the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Walker). I congratulate him on his eloquent and sentimental address on Canada and its future. He is from a wealthy area of Canada and can afford the luxury of this type of broad thinking. But I am from the Maritimes and am more concerned with matters close at hand. Therefore I hope the house will understand if my remarks are not so full of praise about the budget.
The budget was to be the big effort of the new Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp). Good politician that he is I presume he looked over the last election results. I hope he saw the bitter defeat his party received in the Maritimes and I hope he questioned why. However, that would appear to be all he did because his failure to act on our regional imbalances is not being accepted in the eastern provinces.
The slogans that are prevalent today, "Ban the boom" and "Don't do it now, do it later", mean very little to us. We do not know where the boom is. We do not know what he is talking about that should be delayed. We do not have any idea of this going slow.

April 19, 1966

The Budget-Mr. T. M. Bell
The lack of provisions in the budget to deal with our regional problems has caused the Minister of Finance to fall to the very bottom of the ladder with respect to his political ambitions. He is now the low man. I would venture to say he is just as low as was the former minister of finance, the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Gordon), in the eyes of the people in the Maritimes.
I read in the paper the other day that the minister is going to take a course in Berlitz French in order to achieve his political leadership ambitions. I suggest he go out and get a Berlitz course on the Maritimes because it would do him a lot of good and would be easier than the method he is now using to achieve better regard in the Maritimes and to further the ambitions which he quite rightly has.
This problem of regional imbalances is prevalent in many countries of the world. Large and small European countries have had to deal with it. The United States went through a serious period in this respect but has been able to diversify its economy. For example, the motor car industry is located all over the United States. California rivals New York, and the southern states are also well off economically.
It is not an easy problem. It is a difficult challenge to raise the levels of prosperity, particularly in a country with the geography and diversification of Canada. The Maritimes have always been regarded as low income and high unemployment areas. This is not something new. Many figures could be put on the record to illustrate the point.
Lest some people think we are sharing in the current wave of prosperity I point out that in the last five years the regional gain has surpassed the national increase only on three occasions. This might promote false optimism, but so far in the current upswing of the business cycle regional income has not benefited to the same extent as has Canadian income generally. Since 1961-the current expansion began in the first part of that year-personal income has risen 20.1 per cent in the region compared with 22.8 per cent in the nation.
So far as unemployment is concerned I need not give the figures except to say that since world war II unemployment in the Atlantic provinces has been 70 per cent above the Canadian average. Speaking of the postwar period reminds me that it was always said, "You Maritimers have no optimism. You are grovelling around with your problems

without looking to the future". This might have been true but around 1950 we developed a new outlook. As the saying goes, we tried to pick ourselves up by our own bootstraps.
The first measure that we fought for-I see the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), a former premier of New Brunswick, is in his place and he will know what I mean-was the Beechwood project. To my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, that was the first time a federal government assisted a region of Canada in a particular way, and that was the Conservative government of 1957.
The premiers of the Atlantic provinces caught this spirit of optimism, held meetings and introduced constructive proposals on a non-partisan basis. APEC was formed as an agency to gather information which made possible many of the political decisions that were required. Further, the Conservative government set up the Atlantic Development Board, a very revolutionary measure which has had considerable success, and I give the present government credit for modifying it.
A lot more needs to be done, but that was the picture at that time in the Maritimes. At the grass roots and at the political level we were showing new enthusiasm and were trying to do something about our problems. The idea caught on in Ottawa. The Economic Council of Canada was formed and we were optimistic. I digress, Mr. Speaker, for a minute to pay tribute to the work of that council and particularly to Dr. John Deutsch who has shown able leadership. I have always admired him and I particularly admired him for a forthright speech which he delivered to the Canadian Club in Fredericton on January 20, 1966, of which I shall have more to say later.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
Dr. Deutsch set as one of the objectives of the Economic Council the study of how "national economic policies can best foster the balanced economic development of all areas of Canada." They admit there is some difficulty in getting at these deep-rooted problems, but one thing was done. They attacked the system of subsidies and their short term benefits. This advice was given to the Minister of Finance in a very straightforward way by Dr. Deutsch and others but he paid no heed to the part of that advice relating to regional plans. I shall return to this subject later.
Many people of the Maritimes at all levels as well as civil servants here in Ottawa have
April 19, 1966

tried to help in regard to our present difficulty. I should like to pay tribute to those civil servants in Ottawa with whom I have had some communication during the years regarding the problems now facing the Maritimes because, without exception, they showed an interest and a willingness to help us with our difficulties. Every one of them, particularly those of the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Finance, were sincere in their efforts to find a solution.
During the last two years we have been discouraged by the fact that the government has undermined the efforts of all concerned by turning a completely deaf ear and cold shoulder to our representations. Many of us expected that bad news would be forthcoming and we were not wrong in this regard. The metropolitan areas of Halifax, Saint John and Fredericton were excluded from the benefits to be received through the Department of Industry in relation to incentive area plans. This matter has been mentioned in this house on many occasions. Delegations have made representations and briefs have been presented to the government, but the same old stalling has continued.
APEC, which is one of the strongest voices in the Atlantic provinces, has recommended that the entire Atlantic region be included in the new incentive plans. In support of that recommendation let me state that in my own area, the city of Saint John, we are not only failing to receive new industry but are losing some of our old and well established firms because they are moving outside the excluded area.
In addition to the fact that the areas to which I made reference were not included as designated areas, the Minister of Finance has ignored the words of advice of Dr. Deutsch and others. Where is the regional assistance that we were led to expect would be forthcoming and where, to quote the words of Dr. Deutsch, is the "set of policies selected and specifically tailored to promote a rate of growth in this region which is significantly faster than in the country as a whole?"
Tight money policy is making a comeback but the only thing the Minister of Finance has done to assist our region is to pick out a small area of "inflation" in Prince Edward Island and in Westmorland for special attention. He stamped out that inflation by delaying for some time the construction of a causeway. Instead of giving that area a tonic the government has given it a tranquilizer.

The Budget-Mr. T. M. Bell
At this stage I should like to put forward certain proposals. As could be expected, I believe that the entire area of the Atlantic provinces, particularly Halifax, Saint John and Fredericton, should be included in the designated areas. I do not think our difficulties will be solved until that has been done. The government has suggested that the Atlantic Development Board will deal appropriately with this matter. However, success will not be achieved when two different agencies are involved in such an important industrial problem as the one now existing in the Atlantic provinces. I should like to quote again from the speech made in Fredericton by Dr. Deutsch. He said:
-we must take advantage in each region of the trend toward the growing concentration of economic activity in the relatively larger urban centres. This has been a major feature of the pattern of development in all industrially advanced countries. Increasing urbanization has brought new problems which call for new solutions. But to try to reverse this trend would involve much greater economic problems and costs, if indeed it were possible at all.
Many resource-based industries will continue to find advantages in locating close to the resources on which they are based, but we shall also have to offer greater encouragement to development of efficient growth centres within the different regions of our country, including the Atlantic provinces, so that they may be able to develop with the advantages of the vital economies of scale, lower costs, larger markets, and more useful pools of skills.
Those are very significant words and I wish the Minister of Industry (Mr. Drury) were here to listen and pay attention to them.
My second proposal has been mentioned by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton). He stated that different industries and different areas should be exempted from the budget proposals. Some individuals have suggested that this would be selective budgeting. I do not care what name you attach to it, but one thing is certain, the Industrial Development Bank is not giving the Atlantic provinces their pro rata share of assistance.
In this regard, Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out these facts of interest. The people of the Atlantic provinces received 166 of the 2,209 loans made during 1965, or 7.5 per cent. Of the $96,146,000 lent in that year the Atlantic provinces received only $6,016,000, or 6.2 per cent. The average loan made in that area during that year was $36,000.
The Nova Scotia voluntary planning board prepared an excellent report on economic planning and I should like to quote a portion
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. T. M. Bell of that report regarding proposals on monetary and fiscal policy. The report states in part:
In periods of national monetary restraint, and in the absence of excessive aggregate demand pressures in Nova Scotia, the federal government should make an effort to exclude the province from the full force of credit restrictions by (a) having the agencies of the federal government which provide credit, such as the Industrial Development Bank and the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, apply restrictive policies less severely in the province, and (b) encouraging the commercial banks to exempt the province from the full force of restrictions on credit availability.
Evidently that advice did not reach the ears of the minister when he was preparing his famous budget.
My third proposal came to mind when I listened to a question asked today in the house regarding the so-called automobile agreement. This involves an interesting experiment. I do not know what its ramifications are or whether it will or will not help certain areas, but it is evident that the Windsor area, which had employment difficulties, has experienced certain success. I should like to see a similar experiment carried out in respect of particular commodities in the Atlantic provinces area. I think many of our natural markets in the New England states and in the West Indies could be further developed in this way. Let us hope that the next experiment in free trade of this kind is carried out in the Atlantic provinces.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
I put forward these proposals to the Minister of Finance with all sincerity, hoping that he will in some way interest himself in them and redeem himself after the fiasco which he brought forward the other night as his first budget. It is for these reasons that we in the Maritimes are so concerned about the budget. We are concerned about the lack of consideration it displays for our particular area. As I said, beginning in the 1950's we supplied new interest and enthusiasm. Planning boards and agencies were set up, the premiers met, delegations came to Ottawa. Within its responsibility the federal civil service supplied research and information, and action was taken by the previous government.
I ask hon. members to remember Beech-wood, the Atlantic adjustment grants and the Atlantic Development Board. The great regional disparities were there before us. We all joined the battle and the fight was begun. But now the Liberals are back and, in the words of many Maritimers, Ottawa is up to
IMr. Bell (Saint John-Albert).]
its old tricks. Can we afford to turn back the clock to 1956? Is it the old Liberal gang that is letting us down? Will the leopards change their spots?
I am surprised that the Minister of Finance, a former respected civil servant who should have the same interest in this problem that the civil service generally has, and his government do not believe in the principle of special treatment for regional needs. They have become the apologists for big business and central, industrial Canada with all its great power and wealth. For this reason, although the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue made a very good speech it did not interest me.
I call on all members from the Atlantic provinces, regardless of their political affiliation, to unite in putting forward our cause as strongly and forcibly as possible. In this connection we can take a lesson from Quebec. I see some of the members from that province in the chamber. When a question of their just entitlement is involved, when economic objectives are concerned, all of them stand together regardless of party. There is no division along political lines, and one would not dare oppose them. They know what they want; they unite, go forward and get it. Let us do the same and once and for all show the political leaders of this country-I include the Minister of Finance-regardless of their ambition or background, that we really mean business.
I have read the subamendment of the New Democratic Party. Personally I would not support it because it involves the principle of a guaranteed annual income and I have not fully made up my mind on that point. I cannot decide whether this should apply to people who are not working. I also believe that the whole subamendment is premature in view of the report of the Carter commission for which we are waiting.
