speechtext: It would be very good for the Maritimes.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Economic White Paper for 1966, which was tabled in this house shortly before the budget was brought down, makes it abundantly clear that during the year 1965 the economic climate in Canada changed from one of moderate expansion in the early part of the year to what the paper describes as a boom climate at the beginning of the year 1966. In this connection I am not going to take the time of the house to read the
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson unprecedented figure might have been surpassed if the over-all economic expansion had not diverted investment funds into other opportunities.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
However, as my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), has reminded us more than once during recent weeks, it is significant, most significant, in fact, that the current period of exceptional prosperity, our longest period of unbroken prosperity since world war II, shows no sign of abating. Herein lies Canada's immediate problem. Until very recently, the exceptional high and persistent level of demand for goods and services in Canada could be met by our expanding resources and by drawing upon our idle capacity in our factories and the unduly high, in fact alarmingly high, manpower surplus which existed when this government took office just three years ago.
Over the past year or so, however, Mr. Speaker, it has become increasingly apparent that the persistent demand pressures have begun to exceed our supply of manpower and our ability to meet a very difficult situation, at least, to meet it without very serious acceleration in costs and prices. This is something that we in a free economy have to guard against, must guard against, not only because it can impair our world trading position but because damage can be done to prices. This would have a very serious effect on the distribution of incomes.
The Minister of Finance has referred in his Budget speech, clearly and forcefully, to some of the more significant storm signals with which we in Canada are now confronted. He has outlined also some imaginative and constructive steps that the government is taking to help control the situation and to help guarantee continued expansion of the economy. As the minister aptly put it, now is the time to ease off on the gas pedal a little, though there is no need to put on the brakes.
On March 21, when this house was discussing supply, the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) issued a stern warning, a timely one, I agree. He said that inflation signals were flying everywhere, and in a very sad tone of voice he added that the government seemed unaware of the danger. However, Mr. Speaker, the imaginative and carefully thought out Budget that was announced just a week after this speech shows what a very poor analyst the right hon. gentleman really is. I hope that the Budget has reassured him, for it is now evident that
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson the government also had seen the inflation signals, probably long before he had, and that as a matter of fact the government had been giving the problem careful thought for some time so it was and is prepared to act decisively to cope with the dangerous situation to which the right hon. gentleman referred.
Hon. members may perhaps be reminded that the Leader of the Opposition said in effect that government action should be fully applied to all over-spending in Canada. In this connection I might refer to the passage at the bottom of page 2943 and continued on page 2944 of Hansard on that subject. In that same speech, on page 2944 of Hansard, the hon. gentleman refers to a statement by Bruce Hutchison as reported in the Ottawa Journal of February 26, in which the author had stressed the necessity for keeping our prices in line with world prices. The right hon. gentleman's remarks were as follows:
Here Is an article by Bruce Hutchison. No one can ever accuse him of admiring anything more than he admires the present government. This is what he says as reported in the Ottawa Journal of February 26:
"The risk, of course, is that we shall price our goods out of the world market when we have a special chance to price them in."
Then he says, "So I could continue". I think, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members might be reminded that in a subsequent article in the Vancouver Sun of April 4, as well as in other Canadian newspapers, Mr. Hutchison commented on this passage in Hansard to which I have just referred. Perhaps it might not be inappropriate for me to quote Mr. Hutchison's comments on that speech in the house. In this article Mr. Hutchison says:
Indicting the Pearson government for its failure to prevent inflation, Mr. Diefenbaker cites me as a witness. He quotes certain statements from these columns to prove that even a Liberal of my partisan bias has seen inflation coming for a long time.
Then he tells parliament, with ponderous irony and a straight face, that my evidence against the nation's fiscal policies must be taken seriously because there is nothing on earth that I admire so much as the government.
This is kind, tender and very touching. After all the hard things I have written about Mr. Diefenbaker his compassion often fills me with remorse but I fight it down in the interests of truth. And as a man equally devoted to the truth Mr. Diefenbaker will be the first to admit an error.
Farther down he says, referring to Mr. Diefenbaker:
He is wrong in saying that there is nothing I admire as much as the government. No, I admire much more the economic revelations of Mr. Diefenbaker.

They are not of the commonplace, grubby sort learned at college. They don't depend on arithmetic or any sordid reports from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
They emerge, immaculate, out of the deep, poetical subconscious, a sudden spurt of genius repealing the old outworn shibboleths, cancelling the obsolete law of supply and demand, burying Adam Smith, Maynard Keynes and all the economists forever.
When Mr. Diefenbaker gets going on the problems of inflation the spectator stands aghast before a primitive, shattering spectacle of nature, like a sunset on the Arctic tundra or the Matterhorn in moonlight.
There has been nothing so majestic and magical since Coleridge walked the road to Xanadu and found the woman wailing for her demon lover. You can hear those same wails in parliament today.
Having read Mr. Diefenbaker's speech in Hansard, I am too shaken to do it justice. The policy of stringent economy combined with vast new expenditures, the immediate tax reduction designed to cool the overheated business cycle, the need of more money in everybody's pocket to reduce the appetite for goods-these feats of subliminal fantasy leave a man dumb and prostrate in reverence.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I may say also that earlier in this debate the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) said he could find nothing good to say about the Budget. For some reason that I find difficult to understand, he failed to recognize the imaginative, courageous and pioneering features of this Budget which he described as inept and bureaucratic. In the speeches to which I have referred, both the hon. member for Perth and the Leader of the Opposition quoted widely from selected newspaper editorials in an attempt to find support for their position. In view of this, it might be fitting for me to give the house just one quotation from an impartial outside observer, the New York Times.
This highly respected newspaper, in its editorial comment on the first Budget of the Minister of Finance, said:
In taking these steps Mitchell Sharp, Canada's new Finance Minister, is displaying both imagination and flexibility in fiscal policy. Mr. Sharp made clear that his tax package is not intended to halt the upward movement of the Canadian economy. Instead, it is designed to sustain the expansion by moderating it.
In the same editorial I find the following:
The most interesting feature of Mr. Sharp's decision is his innovation of a refundable tax on corporate profits. This proposal represents a flexible attempt to influence corporate spending .... This kind of fiscal flexibility, which has been used in Europe, has been talked about in Washington. Now that Ottawa has introduced it on this side of the Atlantic, Washington too may be encouraged to adopt a more flexible stance.
April 13, 1966

[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
As one who for approximately two decades, Mr. Speaker, was active in two major Canadian industries and also in the public utilities field, I have no hesitation in joining with the Times and with many other leading newspapers in stating that the Budget is not only flexible but it is imaginative, timely and sound. This key approach is to move some demands forward in order to even out the level of business activity.
As has been pointed out in this debate, in the last report of the Economic Council the council warned that the recent rate of expansion and investment spending in Canada is clearly not sustainable on a long range basis. In view of this, Mr. Speaker, may I ask how any intelligent, well informed person can seriously argue that this budget will not relieve at least some of the excessive demands on the economy?
In his comments on the budget the hon. member for Perth also referred to page 7 of a pamphlet entitled "Private and Public Investment in Canada, Outlook 1966." His remarks are reported at page 3729 of Hansard and he quotes from page 7 of the pamphlet as follows:
Within the goods producing industries the greatest additional strength appears in the resource based forest and minerals industries where outlays are expected to increase by one-third compared with the 14 per cent rise recorded last year. Of particular significance are the programs currently planned by the mining industry. These involve a doubling of expenditures in iron mines and a similar increase in outlays for potash mines. In addition, spending for facilities for non-ferrous metal mines is expected to rise by about 50 per cent. The added strength in the forest based industries is entirely the result of a further substantial expansion of investment for pulp and paper mills, involving outlays some $120 million greater than those of 1965.
Then the hon. member goes on to ask this question:
Does the minister want to stop this? These industries help our foreign exchange position; they provide employment and expansion.
In answer to the hon. gentleman's question, Mr. Speaker, it is safe to say clearly and positively that the government does not want to curtail desirable expansion in the forest industry or in any other industry where immediate expansion in these industries is likely to be in the national interest. But what the hon. member for Perth seems to forget is that the forest based and certain other industries in Canada are faced with considerable over-expansion at this particular time, and
The Budget-Mr. Nicholson this is particularly true of the pulp production capacity of this country.
As some hon. members know, I was associated with Canada's forest industry for some little time before I went into politics and, as hon. members will recall, I had the honour to serve as minister of forestry for a period of approximately one year. I speak with some little knowledge and I can say unequivocally that as a result of the enormous expansion of the pulp and paper facilities which is now under way in Canada, particularly in the pulping industry, not only Canada but other export nations of the world are faced with a huge surplus capacity for almost every kind of pulp for the next six or seven years.
In this connection I might refer hon. members to a study which was made in Rome by FAO in the fall of 1963 when I headed the Canadian delegation to the conference held there and my deputy minister chaired the international group who made a study of forecast forest products through to 1975. This review showed conclusively that there will be a huge surplus of certain forest products for the period 1967-1973, followed by shortages in or about 1975.
The forest industry of this country is looking forward to this increased demand in 1975. A great deal of planned expansion in most forest industry activities, however, will not be needed for another five to seven years. That is with the possible exception of newsprint of which there is a shortage. Yet in spite of these figures and in light of the facts brought out in the international study in which representatives from Canada took an active part, at the time the Budget was presented, Mr. Speaker, new pulp and paper capacity representing an investment of approximately $500 million, perhaps more, was either under construction or on the drawing board in British Columbia alone. Other such plants valued at hundreds of millions of dollars were either under construction or on the drawing board in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland. Still others are in the planning stage. I can show hon. members these plants and the forecasts of production and surplus capacity. What the minister is doing in this Budget, Mr. Speaker, is to encourage the owners of plants which will not be needed for two, three, four, five or perhaps seven years to defer construction where it seems wise to do so until closer to the period of anticipated shortage in the 1970's. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, there is little
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson point in building plants at a time when we are short of labour, particularly skilled labour, and when we are short of funds, to meet a demand that is not going to be here for several years.
I can state quite frankly that if I were still in business the fact that after March 31, 1968 there will be no sales tax whatever payable on production machinery and equipment would be a very great inducement for me to defer at least some expenditures of that nature. This is especially true, Mr. Speaker, when you consider that the complicated machinery and equipment in a modern factory, such as a pulp or a paper mill, represents the bulk of the huge expenditures involved. Some of these plants are running into $85 million to $100 million, nearly two-thirds of which cost is for machinery and equipment. Why in the name of common sense should one not wait until there is no sales tax payable on that machinery and equipment?
But, Mr. Speaker, in addition to the inducements or incentives which are provided for in the Budget the federal government itself is easing the pressure-taking some pressure off the gas pedal, if I may use my colleague's words

by reducing its own expenditure program for existing and planned capital projects by some 10 per cent. True, some people, including some members of this house, say that the government could and should have gone farther along this line. But I ask hon. members just to keep in mind that the minister said there was not to be a sudden application of brakes but rather a slowing down. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, a reduction of 10 per cent in anticipated capital spending, representing a postponement of several hundred million dollars, is a slowing down that should set a good example both to private industry and to provincial and municipal governments.
Surely the provinces and some municipalities at least can assist in this slowing down process by carefully examining their planned construction programs with a view to seeing just what projects may be lengthened or what projects can be postponed for a year or two. A postponement of at least some public projects would, I believe, certainly be highly desirable in my own province of British Columbia.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
In addition to the private investment slated for this year, which I have already said is running into hundreds of millions of dollars, there are two large provincial hydroelectric projects in B.C. each running to a total of at


least two-thirds of a billion dollars. The costs of each of these projects have skyrocketed since they were first announced. The ever-increasing payrolls which reflect the recent high wage levels in the province of British Columbia are, I can assure all hon. members, a source of grave concern to private industry in my province. Private industry in British Columbia is finding it increasingly difficult to compete with the tempting wages being paid by the provincial government agency concerned and by its contractors.
In this connection I was gratified to read just a few days ago that the premier of British Columbia, who is certainly a great optimist and who had some critical remarks to make about the Budget when it was first presented, made a statement on April 9 in which he expressed grave concern over the inflationary situation that was developing in the province. He is now suggesting caution in language not very different from that used by the Minister of Finance.
May I read two passages from the Vancouver Sun of April 9, 1966. The headline is: "Bennett Asks Restraint To Halt Inflation". I quote his words from the body of the article:
This Is a dangerous period we're in now . . . . It is an inflationary period and it is not a time at which management should try to make excessive profits nor for labour to make excessive demands.
Farther down he says:
We want to keep this dynamic society of ours moving-
Might one not think that these are the words of the Minister of Finance rather than the premier of British Columbia?
But, Mr. Speaker, while adequate and appropriate fiscal and monetary measures are important and very necessary tools for use in keeping our expanding economy on an even keel, the solution of our other economic and social problems must also be kept in mind. In fact, some such needs must be vigorously pressed. Vast sums of money must be paid out for greater assistance to those who need it. I refer to programs like the Canada Assistance Plan. Vast sums of money are needed for education and vast sums are needed for health purposes. The Minister of Finance made this very clear in this Budget presentation, even though some hon. members opposite who have spoken seem to have overlooked this fact completely.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) in his remarks on April 1 referred to the war on poverty as "government whitewashing." It is hard to
April 19, 1966

believe, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member is serious. Perhaps his statement to which I have referred, having been made on April 1, April fool's day, was intended to be taken with a grain of salt.
The existing activities of the government, which it has been made clear are to continue, include a vast expansion of the technical and vocational training facilities built during the past five years, the rural rehabilitation and development agency, the $112 million housing and electrification program for our Indian communities, area development for industry and vocational rehabilitation for the handicapped. No one, Mr. Speaker, can seriously call the expenditure of $112 million for this very proper and very essential purpose mere whitewashing.
Among other new activities also provided for, which are also to continue, which have been included in this year's estimates and therefore in the Budget are programs of manpower mobility, the development of special experimental training programs for people in areas where opportunity is lacking, an expansion of area development to include capital cost grants to new industries of a fifth to a third, and the expansion of the ARDA program to include a $50 million fund to finance projects in rural areas where poverty is severe. Again, Mr. Speaker, these programs can hardly be referred to as mere government whitewashing. Included also in the war on poverty are the Canada Assistance Plan, recently placed on the order paper, and the Company of Young Canadians, now being established.
True, some of these activities lie ahead. However, in the face of such programs it is hard for me to understand, and I am sure it is difficult for most hon. members in this house to understand, how any responsible member can say that the government is prepared to discard our poor, our handicapped, our unemployed and our untrained as defective parts of the machine.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands at one point in his remarks actually painted Canada as little better than a disaster area. He mentioned slums, poverty and waste of manpower. That there have been problems and serious problems, in some of these areas is true. But what is more important, Mr. Speaker, is that steady progress is now being made to surmount them. Our improved youth allowances program, our increased university grant program, our student loan program and the Canada Pension

The Budget-Mr. Nicholson Plan are good examples of progress. They are certainly not mere whitewashing on the part of the government.
We all know that the provinces have been making enormous efforts to gear their educational systems to our modern needs. We all know that the federal government has been backing up the provinces, especially in areas of technical and vocational training and higher education generally.
Since 1961, when the present technical and vocational training agreements with the provinces came into force-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank hon. members for their courtesy. I am almost through and I will not be very long.
As I was saying, since 1961, when the present technical and vocational training agreements with the provinces came into force, the federal government has shared with the provinces in capital expenditures on more than 860 projects for building and equipping technical and vocational schools. Just within the last year enrolments in all the programs under these federal-provincial agreements have increased by 300 per cent. Those are things that people ought to bear in mind before they start talking about government whitewashing.
In the setting of this Budget debate and in the light of our current problems, Mr. Speaker, it might have been appropriate for me to devote some time and thought to the role that our system of labour relations can and should play in contributing to Canada's social progress and continued economic growth. It has seemed to me for some time that we in Canada have been entirely too reluctant and hesitant in breaking new ground in the solution of broad economic and social problems through the combined efforts
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Brand of labour, management and governments. What we need today, in my opinion, is a new strategy of labour relations in Canada to ensure that economic growth is achieved and that its benefits are fairly shared.
In spite of the indulgence extended by the house, time does not permit me to develop this theme adequately during this debate. I hope to do so, however, on another occasion at an early date. In the meantime I urge hon. members to study and restudy the Budget proposals. When they have done so I have no doubt whatever that both the amendment and the subamendment will receive scant support when the time comes to vote on them.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I rise to speak in the Budget debate perhaps I may be permitted, since it is the first opportunity I have had, to congratulate you and your colleagues on your elevation to the high positions you hold in this house. Coming so many months late, my congratulations may possibly carry a greater note of sincerity, especially after having watched you perform your duties.
I should like, if I may be permitted to do so, to pay a very brief but very sincere tribute to my predecessor in the House of Commons, Dr. Eloise Jones, who served the constituency of Saskatoon with such excellence. Now and for many years to come she will be held in high regard and affection not only by those in this house but also by her constituents in the city of Saskatoon.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
After spending a few days in my home riding, as most members did, I came back to Ottawa having listened to many of my constituents. I received many telephone calls from them and talked with many of them personally. There were many letters waiting on my desk when I returned expressing disappointment because nothing had been done in the Budget to curb the increasing cost of living which is presenting such a serious and real problem to the average Canadian.
I have also received, as I am sure members of the government including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) have, many letters from those unfortunate people who are caught in the cost-price squeeze, people who live on fixed incomes, old age pensioners, for example, for whom no relief is in sight. It disturbed me that there was nothing specifically laid out in the Budget to help solve their serious problem.

At the same time I was disturbed that there appeared to be a lack of proposals to increase the supply of doctors and medical schools in the light of suggestions for a medical care plan applicable to this great country of ours. This situation has prompted me to offer some advice to the government, possibly gratuitous, with regard to a field about which I believe I have some slight knowledge, that is to say, the education and training of doctors and, in particular, of general practitioners, and to suggest means by which we can make use of existing facilities to train more doctors without incurring tremendous expenditures. I consider the present shortage of doctors to be a serious problem. The national need for physicians, particularly for general practitioners, is increasing daily. Along with the necessity to satisfy this need comes something which is just as important-the responsibility of the government as well as of the profession to see that a high quality of medical care continues even as the ranks are thinned. I should like to direct my remarks specifically to the general practitioner, the so-called family doctor, and refer briefly by way of background to his status among his fellows, his opportunities or lack of them, his continuing education and his role in the health team of today.
Perhaps it would be wise first to place this problem in its proper perspective. It is difficult for most of us to realize the immense advances which have been made in medical science as well as in the other sciences in the past half century. In the area of organization and quality control of medicine it was only in 1910 that the Flexner Report made its impact on the United States and Canada, and only in 1912 that Sir Thomas Ruddick fathered the Canada Medical Act, one of the first attempts at organization and quality control of the practice of medicine. It was as recently as 1929 that the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada was formed to help organize the specialists who were springing up as a result of the advances of the day.
However, with these changes in the organization of medicine came the trickle that became a stream and the stream that became a torrent of advances in medical knowledge. Dr. Raymond Keating, professor of medicine at the Mayo Clinic post-graduate school, pointed out the remarkable fact that 90 per cent of all advances in scientific knowledge, including medical science, have taken place during the past ten years by scientists living
April 19, 1966

at the present time. This avalanche of advances has had a profound and lasting effect on medical practice.
As I mentioned before, specialists within medicine were created, five main ones at first and 24 sub-specialties. This was a very necessary and important development in view of the amount of knowledge which was so vast that no one man could grasp more than a small amount of it. This, of course, had other effects. The conscientious family doctor has striven mightily to keep up but has found himself swallowed up in this avalanche, his status and duties becoming more attenuated as the years went by.
The public too have become confused. Surrounded by these advances and anxious to seek the very best care available, they have in many instances sought out specialists directly for medical care, services that few if any specialists have the training and experience to provide.
The medical schools too have undergone a change. Whereas they used to educate doctors for general practice, they now aim to produce what they term a basic undifferentiated doctor. After graduation it is easy for specialist training to be obtained in excellent schools throughout the world, but this does not hold true for general practitioners, although very recently attempts have been made to correct this gap in their continuing education. Little, if any, initiative has been taken by the medical schools to come to grips with the problem.
It is true that brief post-graduate courses are held in an ostensible attempt to continue the education of the general practitioner but these are little more than sounding boards for the lecturers involved. A few of the more enlightened universities have included general practitioners on their faculties, albeit in the lowly positions, but even these attempts have been half-hearted and would seem intended more to quiet the agitated general practitioner than to elevate his intellect. The result of this has been that since our medical knowledge has a half life of ten years or, to put it another way, one half of one's knowledge is replaced by new knowledge in ten years time, specialists have become better with all the facilities available to them. Meanwhile, however, the general practitioner has become in the eyes of his peers a second-class doctor or, in that faintly contemptuous phrase, "only a general practitioner".

The Budget-Mr. Brand
Despite all this, the family doctor of today is better trained than he has ever been, and with the facilities he has at hand he is better able now to diagnose and treat disease than he has ever been. The dedicated general practitioner works harder on the average for longer hours and for much less pay than the great majority of his specialist colleagues. This is something I should like the government to take a close look at if they wish to maintain a high level of medical care as they develop schemes for medical care across this country.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The lack of continuing training for the family doctor has resulted in the gradual closing of hospitals. I do not mean the closing of beds or of front doors; I mean in the medical sense of restricting those who are admitted to hospital staffs. I mean the limiting and restricting of privileges of general practitioners who by some stroke of fate are still allowed to practice in the precincts of a particular hospital. In Britain we have the ultimate result of family doctors practising completely apart from the hospitals, becoming office and home doctors with no opportunity to practise continuing care for their patients. This was clearly pointed out at the first international conference of Colleges of General Practice, which was held in Canada at the behest of our College of General Practice in 1964. At that conference general practitioners from Britain and other countries which have followed this same type of practice very clearly pointed out the trend.
In many areas of our own country the general practitioner is still allowed to practise within his competence in our hospitals but every day more and more these privileges are being whittled away. In the university centres, except for the few enlightened ones -they are few, I can assure you-such as the University of Alberta, at Calgary, the University of Western Ontario at London, and Dalhousie in Halifax, except for those which have pilot projects coming up this year the general practitioner is being squeezed out of hospital work under the guise that his continuance would only lower the standards of medical care.
By some strange process of reasoning the majority of our medical educators today seem to believe that you can elevate the standards of medical care by excluding almost totally from the centres of learning those who look after between 85 per cent and 90 per cent of
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. Brand the health care of Canada. They do this without seeing what is obvious to me, that by free association with the very best in medical care, by rubbing shoulders and practising alongside those who represent the finest in specialist care, and by having their work scrutinized by these same people, our standards of care could not help but rise to meet and face the challenge that would be their's. This is something that our medical educators do not seem to understand.
We hear the pious platitudes of these same educators who say, and I have heard them, that their primary purpose is to train general practitioners because we have such a need of them and because we shall need more and more of them due to all the medical care programs that are coming along. They say this publicly but at the same time they do their utmost to downgrade the work of the family doctor and expose the medical student to a totally specialist or fragmented atmosphere where the patient becomes lost in the shuffle and becomes an interesting case rather than a human being afflicted with disease.
Hospitals even outside the university setting are becoming increasingly departmentalized and with this the privileges of the general practitioner on staff are becoming increasingly restricted, even in areas of already demonstrated competence.
There is no question in my mind that those who perpetuate this state of affairs are sincere in their objectives, but there is also no question in my mind that they are very wrong in what they seek to achieve. They are not entirely to blame. The general practitioner himself has become so used to being a second-class medical citizen that in many instances he has given in and has watched his privileges being whittled away without a murmur.
Others, however, in the general practitioner group, with the encouragement of some of the more enlightened specialists, have tried to break through the indifference that has settled on general practice. In 1954 they set up the College of General Practice of Canada with the objectives of stimulating postgraduate training, research and teaching in their chosen field. This college was incorporated in 1960 and has as its motto, "In education lies our strength." This group certainly recognizes the necessity of doing something now to try to produce more general practitioners to meet the needs in Canada today.
TMr. Brand.]

I should like to quote briefly, if I may, Dr. Rice who is executive director of the College of General Practice of Canada.
Is it not paradoxical in the presence of a demonstrated need for more family doctors, to have a decline in the number of general practitioners who are leaving practice for other endeavours, and in the numbers of newly-graduated doctors entering general practice as a career? Why has this situation developed? To those who study this problem, the answer is obvious and should surprise no one. Simply, we-
By "we" he means the general practitioners as well as the medical professors.
-have not kept pace with present community needs. We have failed to keep up to date by adapting the present day pattern of general practice to meet these needs, and more seriously we have given up training medical students as family doctors. We have permitted a situation to develop where general practice has been allowed to become in the eyes of many, and in particular in the eyes of the medical student, that which remains in the practice of medicine once the specialities have been extracted from it.
We have permitted the general practice of medicine to become increasingly unattractive by allowing it to become a way of life which is more restrictive in its scope, more demanding in terms of time, lacking in recognition and prestige, and less remunerative in its monetary return.
The College of General Practice has gone ahead and set up these post-graduate programs. I have mentioned three universities where this year residencies in general practice will be going into effect to help improve the standard of general practice in Canada, and it needs to be improved. It was this same college which commissioned Dr. Kenneth Clute, a specialist from Toronto, to do a study on the general practitioner, to do it without fear or bias and see what was wrong with the profession in Canada and what could be done about it. These residencies I have mentioned are training programs which are being set up and they are a step in the right direction. But the point is that the College of General Practice is still going to be stymied in its ultimate objective unless we awaken our medical schools and make them realize that they must integrate fully into their cur-riculums the general practice of medicine.
It is no longer good enough for them to say that this cannot be done. Such arrogance can only hurt the practice of medicine in the future. They must recognize that they have a direct responsibility and be willing to act on this responsibility. You can give medical schools as much money as you want, but until they change the manner in which they are training their doctors you are not going to
April 19. 1966

maintain the standard of medical care or increase the number of doctors who are going to be needed in future years.
Hospitals too must realize that it is no longer good enough to departmentalize into departments of medicine or surgery, or what have you, or clinical departments where patients are treated and then, in order to keep the family doctor from making too much fuss, allow a general practice department which is not in the least bit clinical, which is merely a paper thing where you have a meeting once a year to satisfy some administrative thinking. This does away with the continuing education of general practitioners. It does nothing to boost the sinking morale of the family doctor. It just keeps him from raising too much fuss at the local medical meetings.
With the prospective need for doctors in our country it is up to the government to give direction to the medical schools and to hospitals to encourage the continuing education of the general practitioner and help break down the ivory tower bastions that have been set up in so many of our medical schools. We can turn out more doctors without building too many more medical schools. We have countless community hospitals ready and available now in which the integrated training of doctors can be carried out in co-operation with our medical faculties. What we need are medical teachers. We need more teachers and facilities to train medical teachers.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
We need more teachers not only in the specialties but teachers in the general practice of medicine, the only practice which looks at the patient as a whole patient rather than just a part. This is the segment of the practice of medicine that is so necessary for the preservation of the human being and human dignity in the presence of disease.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, it will seem quite obvious to everyone that I am somewhat partisan in my remarks, but I think it is high time someone took to task those medical educators and specialists who are so insular in their approach that they consider the average family doctor as someone to be tolerated only and never totally accepted in the great society of Hippocrates.
We need more doctors, primarily family doctors, and unless we change our attitude and integrate general practice into medical schools and hospitals the trend already started, where 60 per cent or more of our medical students go directly into the specialist fields, 23033-2541
The Budget-Mr. Lewis will continue whereas the reverse used to be true. Closed hospitals, limited and restricted privileges and other terms like these should be abolished. In their place should come practices related directly to one's training and one's competence.
In conclusion may I say that the general practitioner agrees with Maimonides in his "Daily Prayer of a Physician":
May there never develop in me the notion that my education is complete, but give me strength and leisure and zeal continually to enlarge my knowledge.
On that note may I make a plea to the government to look very carefully at the problem of medical education. This is something that cannot be swept under the rug in the hope that as a result of establishing a medicare plan it will be solved. This problem will not be solved in this way. We need direction and help from the government and I ask the government to look seriously at this problem to see what can be done to improve the lot of the largest number by far of men educated in the medical profession today.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the general rate of growth of the economy in Canada I wish it were possible to say nice things about the Budget and, more particularly, about the Budget speech, but I do not think that is possible for any objective person studying the social and economic conditions of our country today.
When I read and re-read the minister's speech in introduction of his Budget I came to the conclusion that this Budget decrees that the poor shall, indeed must, always be with us. In his speech the minister bemoaned the fact that inflation hurts the poor the most, and he was right. Rising consumer costs certainly hurt people on low or fixed incomes most of all. But the minister says in effect, we cannot do anything or we can do very little for the poor precisely because of the inflation which hurts them. To me this is not only a vicious circle but a declaration of moral and social bankruptcy on the part of the minister and the government for which he speaks, and indeed of the entire social and economic establishment in Canada.
So is another lamentable implication of the minister's speech, and I challenge him to show where at any place in my general analysis of his words there is an illogical point. His analysis of the economic situation alleges that the reason for the inflationary

April 19, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Lewis pressures, as he insisted throughout his speech, is the fact that we are using our productive capacities to the full or almost to the full.
What does that mean? It means that the minister boasts of our expansion and prosperity and then concludes that he can do nothing substantial for the poor of Canada. I say to him and to you, sir, that there are only two alternative implications to be drawn from this kind of analysis of our economic situation. The first is that we can do more for the poor when we are experiencing a recession, when we do not have inflationary pressures. That is an obvious piece of arrant and cynical nonsense. Or, alternatively, the implication in the minister's analysis is that we can never eliminate poverty in Canada; we cannot do it in times of recession because we do not have enough and we cannot do it adequately in times of prosperity because we have too much.
That is precisely what the minister says in his Budget speech to the poor of this country, and I have no doubt that he will deny any such implications in his speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I was sure that the minister would deny it, but I say to him in all seriousness, because I think this is the basis of the discussion that ought to take place in this parliament and in our country, that whether he denies these implications or not, indeed, whether he intends them or not, they are the only conclusions that can be drawn from the totality of his presentation. Otherwise he would have said to this parliament and to the country that it is precisely because we have such expansion in our economy, and precisely because we are experiencing a period of continued prosperity, that this is the time when the government will take all necessary measures to eliminate poverty.
Furthermore, I say to you that the blind approach which the minister and his government have taken to the social purposes of our economic activity has shown one thing that has always annoyed me beyond words, and that is the ease with which economic experts and ministers of finance point to indices of prosperity and rates of growth, always ignoring the one basis for that growth and that is its social purpose.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me say I am not concerned with economic growth, nor is anyone in my

party, nor should anyone in this house be, if the results of that growth are concentrated in the hands of those who already have too much. That is exactly what has been happening in this country. It is only this blind approach to the social purpose of our economic activity that could have led the minister and his government to commit such a regrettable and repellent hoax on the low income groups as that contained in the minister's manipulations of the income tax provisions.
The minister went into a long song and dance about the fact that even though inflation required him to take back the tax reduction which was made a year ago, or most of it, he was not going to touch the poor people and he was going to make their lot better. After this self-righteous speech, if you look at the tables that he himself included in his budget speech, what do you find? You find that this tremendous generosity on the part of the minister will result in a reduction in taxes for a single person who earns $1,500 a year of $4 per year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much tax did he pay?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That does not matter and it is not relevant.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I think it is.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister says it is relevant and I say it is not relevant, and that proves my point. If these people were unable to pay bigger taxes before it was the fault of the minister and his government because they were not able to earn more money to pay more taxes.
The point with which I am concerned is the ease with which the minister is able to salve his conscience by saying, I am helping the poor. What does this help consist of? It consists of $4 per year for a single man earning $1,500, 33 cents per month or 7J cents per week.
[DOT] (5 .40 p.m.)

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much did they pay in taxes?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The minister has already asked that question and I think I have answered him. I say to him in further answer that he might have been more generous to the people of Canada and more appreciative of their need and would have shown a much more sincere feeling for the poor had he increased old age pensions and established a floor in respect of income instead of perpetrating this
April IS, 1966



insincere hoax which gives a single man $4 per year, 33 cents per month or 7J cents per week, this hoax which gives a married man without dependants earning $2,500 per year $4 per year, 33 cents per month or 7J cents per week. To the married person with two children earning $3,000 a year he gives 5-| cents a week, to the $3,500 a year man, 17 cents a week, to the $4,000 a year man, 9i cents a week. This is the generosity he shows to the poor of Canada. My point is not that he was doing anything completely wrong in reducing taxes for these people; it is that he should have reduced them substantially more. I am making the point that the entire policies should have been directed toward raising the living standards of all the people who pay such low taxes and a third of the people who do not pay any taxes at all.
Despite this, Mr. Speaker, if you look into the record you find that over a year ago, in the 1965 Throne Speech, the government declared a war on poverty; indeed, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) talked about it before the Throne Speech. On April 5, 1965, His Excellency the Governor General read some stirring and ringing words. Some of them are worth recalling. The Throne Speech said:
All the great potentialities of our economy are not, however, being realized. The talents of some of our people are wasted because of poverty, illness, inadequate education and training, inequality in opportunities for work.
I pause here to say that at least the Prime Minister and the government realize that these conditions, which some of us have been drawing to their attention for decades, do in fact exist. The Throne Speech went on to say:
To combat these problems, to improve the opportunities of people who are now at a disadvantage, is to put new power into economic expansion and to enhance the unity of our country.
I applaud that sentiment. Who would not? Everyone in Canada applauded that statement because increasingly we are becoming aware of these things. What are we talking about when we speak of poverty in Canada?
I want to spend a few minutes outlining the elements of poverty directly from a publication of the Special Planning Secretariat that the Prime Minister set up. These figures are contained in a publication called "Meeting Poverty-Profile of Poverty in Canada." The first few pages of this publication contain a summary of the findings of the secretariat. Here you find some really distressing facts which ought to have found their way into the Budget or at least into the Budget speech.
The Budget-Mr. Lewis
You find that in Canada- and this is what we are talking about when we speak of poverty- at the census of 1961 some 23 per cent of Canadian families had an income of less than $3,000 a year. This figure of $3,000 is the line drawn by welfare counsellors and sociologists as the floor for a half-decent standard of living for a family with children. As I say, 23 per cent, one out of every four of our Canadian families, had an income of less than $3,000 a year. In addition some 700,000 single persons made less than $1,500 a year. If you add these numbers together you have some four million Canadians or more than 25 per cent of our people, who are members of families or are single, below the line of income required for a half-decent standard of living. One out of every four Canadians is in that situation.
With regard to families headed by women, says this report, more than half-not 23 per cent but more than half-had incomes of less than $3,000 a year and about two-fifths or 40 per cent of them lived on less than $2,000 a year. If you consider the situation with regard to fishermen, logging and farm workers, you find that three out of five families of fishermen, which is 60 per cent, and every second family of logging and farm workers, which is 50 per cent, and one third of our labourers, which is 33J per cent, had incomes below $3,000 a year. This is the extent of existing and continuing poverty in Canada. This situation is even more striking if you analyse it in some of its various aspects.
In early pages of the same report you find that the unemployment rate among workers under 20 years of age is more than double the national average. Note that this applies to people under 20 years of age, which is precisely the age when we should develop young Canadians into having an appreciation of their country and a desire to make a contribution to it. Yet their unemployment rate is more than double the national average.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, we think of Canada as a country of widespread education. But note this. In 1961, says this report-I am not quoting it but am citing figures from it-of Canadians aged 15 and over there were 5,166,346, or 47 per cent, with no more than elementary schooling. I draw to the attention of the house this figure of 47 per cent of those aged 15 and over who in 1961 had only elementary schooling. These included 176,524 with no schooling at all, and a figure as high as 848,261 with schooling of four grades or

April 19, 1966
The Budget-Mr. Lewis less. These conditions are found in an affluent, expanding economy. These are the facts about the situation in Canada today.
When you come to the aged people, which is the next most helpless group, you find that 21 per cent of Canadians aged 65 to 69 consistently receive old age assistance. That is, almost one out of every four persons aged 65 to 69 receives old age assistance. The median annual income for men in their late 60's is $2,000, $1,500 in their early 70's, and $900 in their late 80's, if they live that long. As they become older, in need of greater income, as their health fails, as they become more helpless, their income is reduced from $2,000 in the late 60's to $900 in the late 80's. How more inhuman and thoughtless can a society be than one which treats its old people this way?
If you look at health, which is the next criterion in the realm of poverty, you find this statement at page 5 of the report:
Low income groups receive less health care than higher income groups, although they suffer from more illnesses in general and their illnesses tend to be more severe.
In housing you find the same story. You find that among families earning $6,000 and over in 1961, only 18 per cent lived in dwellings providing less than a room per person. But among families earning less than $3,000 this proportion was 35 per cent. They also lived, in significant measure, in houses infested with rats and vermin, houses in need of major repair and unfit for any human being to dwell in. This is what we are speaking about when we talk of poverty.
The Canadian Welfare Council prepared a report for the conference on poverty last December. For the purposes of this report they carried out a survey of families in four Canadian cities. In their report the Canadian Welfare Council "painted a bleak picture of poverty among city dwellers". They found that the median income per person for the families studied in Saint John, New Brunswick, and Montreal was $34 a month; in Toronto it was $44 a month and in Vancouver it was $53 a month.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
The majority had less than grade 8 education, insufficient to enable them to get better or more permanent jobs or even to take part in retraining courses. The report stated that housing is a source of deep anxiety for the poor. Few own their own houses and rents are high. Food and rent consume almost 70 per cent of all incomes.

Then there is this sentence in the report:
Sharing the house with rats and other vermin does not give people a sense of their own worth or a wish to be part of the community. Nevertheless, most do want to be part of their neighbourhood and do not want to move away even from these tenuous connections.
The Canadian Welfare Council also stated in a report on rural poverty that Canada's rural poor subsist in some areas on incomes as low as $11.71 per person per month. These are the facts about the Canadian people. I repeat that we are dealing with somewhere between 25 and 30 per cent of Canadians. These are the facts which the minister had before him when he was preparing the Budget.
There is no word in the Budget about the war on poverty. There is nothing to suggest that there are steps being taken that are adequate at the present time. This so-called war on poverty is a paper war. There is not a day but I find on my desk some press release from the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Sauve) about some kind of pilot project which has been established in some part of some province of Canada. By this time I think the minister ought to have enough pilots to get himself at least one ship that knows where it is going and how to get there.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? If I had filled my Budget speech with already announced policies of the government, would he not now be accusing me of having padded it?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, I would not. I would have been delighted if he had been able to find government policies with which to fill his speech. I would have been delighted to listen to a list of government policies to deal effectively with this problem in Canada. Let him not hide behind other government promises. As Minister of Finance, and I shall come to this in a moment if I can, he had certain steps to take with relation to taxes; he had certain steps to take with relation to monetary policy; he had certain steps to take with relation to the fiscal field generally.
He could have taken these steps if he had not been completely blind to the real needs of Canada and if he had not taken off on the usual course of the big business fraternity in this country. All of these factors to which I have referred persist today, as they did in 1961. Of course I agree, as anyone with any sense of integrity at all would agree, that some of the problems will require time to be solved. They cannot be solved by the wave of
April 19, 1966
a wand or the snapping of somebody's fingers. Certainly it takes time to retrain; it takes time to replace illiteracy with some education; it takes time to have industry that will absorb such people. However, precisely because it takes time, Mr. Speaker, and I cannot help but become angered by this kind of excuse from the other side, the longer you delay the start the longer it will take to find a solution and the longer these people will continue to suffer. The start that has been made is a picayune and pusillanimous one which does not even approach the problems with which we are faced. Hence the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, because as one expert in the United States said some time ago, and I do not recall his name, many people forget the simple proposition that the poor need income. It is as simple as that.
It is for this reason we say in our subamendment that people who make as little as $1,500, if they are single, ought not to pay any income tax, and married people, with a family, making only $3,000 ought not to pay any income tax. We ought to begin now to build a guaranteed floor under income for every Canadian in every part of the country. There is no other way in which you can get people out of their poverty except by providing them now with the necessary income to live like decent human beings in self-respect and dignity. Then their attitude will change. Then, and then only, will it become possible to retrain them, to educate them, to make them more productive citizens of our community.
The point is, Mr. Speaker, that in order to do this the Minister of Finance would have had to bring in a Budget which made some drastic and radical redistribution of income from those who have too much to those who have nothing or too little. It is this refusal to recognize the need for using monetary and fiscal policy to redistribute income, including in this case the taking of more power into the hands of the government, that leads the minister to present a Budget which contains relatively nothing at all. If he had had any less, he could not even have made a speech about it, let alone call it a Budget.
The minister is anxious and concerned about inflation. He is so concerned about it that he makes an elementary error in economics unless what I studied in economics in two universities was completely wasted on me. As reported on page 3380 of Hansard the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion minister stated that there would be an increase of rather more than 9 per cent in the gross national product in 1966. Of this, a little more than 5 per cent would be in volume and 4 per cent in price. Then he says:
That is the prediction my advisers made without taking into account any of the proposals that I shall make subsequently. Part of the expected price increase is attributable directly to contributions under the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans and to the recently announced increase in the Ontario provincial sales tax, both of which reflect improvements in public and social services.
There may be some element of validity in the reference to the Ontario provincial sales tax, which is in the short run handed over to the consumer in the form of higher prices. But surely it is sheer nonsense to talk about contributions under the Canada and Quebec Pension Plans as being inflationary. Surely they are the opposite. Surely they are just as much a tax as any other tax, and are deflationary rather than inflationary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am sure the hon. gentleman wants to be fair. I did not say they were inflationary; I said they were the cause of some of the increase in prices.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The minister is either playing on words now or he was playing on words in his Budget speech.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I was being exactly accurate in the Budget speech.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, in the Budget speech the minister dealt with increases in price as being synonymous with inflation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, I did not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, the minister did. In any case, even the statement that they put pressure on prices is an exceedingly questionable one for anyone to make in this house or elsewhere.

Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Monteith, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Cameron (Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands).

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the dinner recess 1 was dealing with the minister's erroneous statement, to be found at page 3380 of Hansard that the contributions to the federal and Quebec pension plans will be directly responsible for part of the price increase he expects in the future. I want to make clear that I did not refer to what I think is an error merely to introduce a minor technical argument, but because it seemed to me to indicate an approach typical of conservative economic thinking which seeks to tarnish the value of welfare measures such as old age pension plans.
Every member of this house is concerned with increased prices. Last year there was an increase of 3.5 per cent. After making long dissertations about the action he was going to take to stop this inflation, the minister ended up by telling us that he hoped-he could not guarantee it obviously-that the expected increase of 4 per cent in the consumer price index might be reduced to 3.5 per cent. After all the effort he expended and all the words he threw at this parliament and the country, he ended up by reducing the inflationary percentage from 4 per cent to 3.5 per cent.
Three point five per cent last year and 3.5 per cent this year will be a 7 per cent increase in the cost of living in two years. This will be disastrous for industrial and agricultural workers generally and those on low and fixed incomes such as old age pensioners, in particular.

What causes these terrible increases in prices, Mr. Speaker? Did the minister bother to ask himself whether they were justified by cost increases or by other genuine and legitimate factors of the market? Should we not find out whether they were justified? Before putting on the brakes, or taking the foot off the pedal, or whatever simile the minister wants to use, should he not have satisfied himself that the price increases came from justifiable economic pressures? I can look only at the available data, and the available data I want to deal with first are the profit increases as compared to the price increases.
It is true that we have had an overall price increase of 3.5 per cent. The largest increase is the rise in food prices. As my hon. friend from Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) pointed out, and as the Canadian Economic Council also pointed out, that was mainly the result of shortages in meat products, fruit and vegetables in the United States.
However, if you look at what happened to profits in the year 1965 you really find an astonishing result. There was an increase in the profits in all industries, as can be seen from a study of any of the publications dealing with this matter, of 13.5 per cent in 1965 over 1964. That was already on top of an increase of 14.6 per cent in 1964 over 1963, which again was on top of an increase of 6.6 per cent in 1963 over 1962, and of 9 per cent in 1962 over 1961.
One might say that 1961 was the year in which the upward curve of the economic cycle started, and therefore you would expect a somewhat higher rate of profit increase to result in 1962; but there is no excuse, other than sheer profiteering, for an increase of 14.6 per cent in 1964 over 1963 and an increase of 13.5 per cent in 1965 over 1964. If you take the five years from 1961 to 1965, the total percentage increase in profits in that period for all industries is 51 per cent.
I was particularly interested to look at the profits in the food and beverages industry, from which some of the particularly large increases in the consumer price index come. I found that in the food and beverages industry there was an increase in profit of 18.5 per cent in 1965 as compared with 1964, which is 5 per cent more than the average increase for all industries in Canada. This is where the price increases on food come from- profiteering by food processing and food packing companies.
April 19, 1966

Taking the five year period 1961-65 there was an increase of 43 per cent in the profits in the food processing and packing industries. The same thing applies to retail trade profits, which show an increase of 20 per cent in 1965 over 1964.
When the subject of profits is referred to in this house, and also outside the house, somebody immediately raises the question: How-about wages? Well, how about wages? If a similar calculation is made with respect to wages-I am referring to total labour income, which includes salaries, wages and other sources of labour income-you find that the increase in 1965 as compared with 1964 was only 11 per cent, as against 13.5 per cent increase in profits. In 1964 it was 8.7 per cent over 1963, compared with 14.6 per cent for profits.

No time limit was set. I do not intend to take advantage of my extension, but I do intend to take enough time to enable me to complete my remarks. I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that if you look at wage increases you will find that only in 1963 compared with 1962 was the percentage wage increase, 6.7 per cent, about the same as the profit increase for that period, namely 6.6 per cent.
Because of the kind of propaganda I have often heard both in this house and outside, I should underline that the important thing when you look at these figures is to realize that they are figures for total labour income. If you look at wages only you will find an increase in 1965 over 1964 of only 5.2 per cent, as compared with the figure of 11 per cent representing the increase in total labour income.
Wages of industrial workers alone-wages which are said to affect prices-increased in 1965, compared with 1964, by only 5.2 per cent. In the manufacturing part of the industrial complex, which of course is the major part as far as value of production is concerned, the increase in 1965 over 1964 was only 4.9 per cent. Remember too, Mr. DEBATES
The Budget-Mr. Lewis Speaker-and I underline this-that these statistics are based on surveys of firms which employ 15 employees or more, they do not cover firms which employ less than 15 employees.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
It is a well established economic fact that the smaller the firm, generally speaking, the smaller the wage rate, and therefore the smaller the wage earnings of the workers. There are exceptions to this, of course, but generally speaking that has been established in economic history. If you take the workers in smaller establishments, particularly in manufacturing industries, the likelihood is that you would find a picture that is worse than the one that has already been given.
Aside altogether from these percentages, Mr. Speaker, the fact is that after you have dealt with all these increases in wages you still have an average weekly wage in Canada, in the industrial composite, of $91.18. That is in Canada as a whole. That is the average. This is not a high wage today, and anyone has the right to complain if he has a family in modern Canada, in 1966, if he is earning that. That is only a total annual income of approximately $4,500, or less, which is about 50 per cent above the poverty line of $3,000 a year which we discussed earlier.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the farmers now?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
When you come to the farmers the statistics for their earnings are made up in a different way. While the increase in food prices has been the most substantial part of the total price increase, as far as I have been able to ascertain from my studies of the situation, it is not the farmer who has received that increase: it is the middle organization, the corporation that packs and processes the farmer's product, that has had the advantage of this increase in price.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands proposed on behalf of this party the subamendment to which I referred earlier and which will be voted on later. It was because of the thinking involved in it that my leader earlier in this session proposed a prices review board to investigate price increases in order to find out whether they are justified.
What the minister should have done, before he condemned the lower economic areas of this country to at least another year of stagnation, before he condemned the people in poverty in this country to continue in their
4014	COMMONS DEBATES	April 19, 1S66
The Budget-Mr. Lewis poverty, is this: He should have satisfied himself how much of the increase in prices is due to administered prices; how much of that increase is due to monopolistic greed; how much is due to a deliberate policy by the corporations to get as much money as the traffic will bear. In short, how much of that increase in prices is due to sheer conscienceless profiteering?
If this is the reason for much of the increase in prices, as I am personally convinced it is, the remedy is not to condemn millions of Canadians to continue living in poverty. The remedy is to take a number of new, brave, logical steps to stop this profiteering, rather than to condemn poor people to continue being poor.
But the minister in his budget was very tender to the corporations. When he imposed a 5 per cent tax on them, he made it refundable. The corporations will pay this refundable tax in monthly instalments over a period of 18 months. At the end of that time, for the following 18 months, he will return it to them with 5 per cent interest.
I was struck by the comparison between the personal income tax, which the minister said, and I am using his figures, meant a total annual addition to revenue of $210 million, none of that being returned to the taxpayer, and this 5 per cent refundable tax which will bring about $250 million a year, but which is to be returned to the corporations with interest. What an eloquent contrast there is in the minister's treatment of the workers and middle class people of this country who pay most of the $210 million that he is going to get in additional money and the way he treats the corporations.
From the corporations he takes this refundable tax in a measure which is just about as useless, and I say that, choosing my words carefully, as anything of which a serious economist could possibly conceive. The $250 million involved in this 5 per cent refundable tax, amounts to about 2 per cent of the total projected investment by private corporations. And, Mr. Speaker, I see no reason in the world why these corporations should not pay the 5 per cent refundable tax into the minister's treasury and invest exactly the same amount as they intended to invest. These corporations never invest the last of their pennies. They always have resources in their undistributed reserves, or from borrowing, if that is what they intended to do. Giving the minister money at 5 per cent, money which in 18 months or 24 months they will get back, is not a bad thing for them. Five per cent is

not a bad return, when all you have to do is let the money lie in the minister's pocket.
Therefore this whole gesture is so phony as to be outrageous. The minister said that this is economic planning. With due respect, it is an example of nothingness of the most meaningless kind.
I will not deal with the Swedish system because my hon. friend the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands has already done so.
I wish to conclude by very briefly suggesting the following measures which are necessary now: I respectfully say to you, sir, and to all hon. members in this house that this budget underlines as few things have done the need for full and courageous planning of Canada's economy.
The minister talks about the construction boom. He talked about it in most of his speech. Sure, there is one. It does not require an economic genius to know that the boom is primarily due to centennial projects across Canada; to Expo '67, and to all the various projects undertaken all across the country. That there is a boom in other building as well I will not deny. But the great pressures on the construction industry, the more than desirable pressures on that industry are due to the building programs of villages, towns, cities, provinces, and the federal government across Canada, having to do with the centennial. Those pressures will end in 1967 or 1968. There is not a word in the budget of any plan to provide a necessary substitute. There is no shelf of building projects except the few things that the minister has deferred in public construction.
We now need more, and not less, expenditure on area development, in order to equalize opportunities in this country, in the way in which the Speech from the Throne said on April 5, 1965 it should be done. We need the Canadian Development Corporation about which not a word appeared in the Throne Speech, and about which there was not a word in the Budget.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

If it is, then I take back what I have said just now. But there is not a word about it in the Budget. And, what is perhaps more important, it is not on the order paper.
Even more significant is the fact that last week end at a Young Liberals Convention one of the senior ministers of the Crown said that he doubted very much whether there

was any value in this development corporation. This was the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Winters). The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) later appeared at the convention and read a lecture on how the corporation was very necessary, and that the government will introduce it.

I am sure it will not be the kind of corporation I would introduce, Mr. Speaker. I am certain that the minister will introduce something similar to the idea that was laid out before us one or two years ago, where 90 per cent of the public corporation was to be in the hands of private corporations. I am sure that in the minister's proposal the government will have very little to do with the policies of this Canadian Development Corporation. Certainly, that is not the kind of proposal that we would introduce. That is not the* kind of thing the New Democratic Party had in mind when it proposed, as it did propose years ago, the Canadian Development Fund-long before it appeared in the Throne Speech of this government.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I go on to say, Mr. Speaker, that we need planning to which public investment is tied in as a necessary instrument all down the line. We need to use the Canadian Development Corporation for the purpose of increasing the public sector in the economy in order that the minister may have much greater control than he has now. At the present time, when he says he intends to reduce public spending on construction by 10 per cent he is talking, as I am sure he will agree, about a very small part of total investment in Canada. The effect of such a reduction upon the economy is almost infinitesimal because of the relatively small amount of expenditure in the public sector of the economy. The greater the investment in public hands, the more the steps which the Minister of Finance takes in future years, the greater will be the effect on the economy as a whole.
