speechtext:
Let the minister try to give some leadership and see what response is forthcoming-not leadership in words, not leadership in speeches on the floor of the house, not leadership in a Speech from the Throne only, but in terms of actual plans with concrete financial propositions, plans the details of which are laid out in such a way that the provinces will know exactly where they are going; not in such a way as to place added financial burdens on the provinces which they are unable to bear.
I say, briefly, that we need legislation to deal with foreign ownership. The Canadian Development Corporation, or Development Fund, is the only effective way to deal with foreign ownership. Again there is not a word about it in this Budget. I was pleased by the compliment the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), a very honourable gentleman, paid to the previous minister of finance, another honourable gentleman. Nevertheless, it was significant that despite these honourable exchanges between honourable men-and I note that the former minister of finance paid the present minister the same kind of courteous compliment-the fact is that many of the things which the former minister of finance considered the cornerstone of Canada's economic future have been forgotten by his successor, particularly with regard to the question of foreign ownership.
We need a policy aimed at redistributing income in Canada to give everyone a fair and adequate income. This means the placing of a floor under income. I say, with all the emphasis I can, that if a prosperous time of economic expansion is not the time for taking these steps to improve the quality of life in Canada, I should like to know when the time will be ripe for this kind of action. This is the time to fight poverty, to take steps to eliminate inequalities in Canada as between groups and regions. It is not a time to stand pat as the minister did in his Budget, or to sit complacently as he does now.
April 19, 1966

The Budget-Mr. Rochon [Translation]

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, allow me to congratulate the previous speaker for his creditable attempt to win us over to his views. But all members of the house realized that the politician gave way to the petty politician, never losing sight of the interest involved: that of his own party.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know exactly how many budgets have been brought down since confederation. A hundred? Perhaps more, perhaps less, because it must be kept in mind that in certain circumstances, twelve months have elapsed without a budget being submitted to the house, as was the case, for instance, during the last year of the administration of our friends opposite, and that some other years, there were more than one, the main budget and the other commonly called the baby budget. Obviously, then, it is difficult to specify, even with all these statistics.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Be that as it may, the bringing down of the budget is always wrapped in mystery. There is in the air an atmosphere of suspense, as it would be called in the film industry, and the other evening, it was surely a good idea to adjourn the house for a little over an hour before the arrival of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp).
Like other government members who spoke previously, I feel duty bound to congratulate him on his masterly report of the situation in Canada; he clearly indicated the soundness of our economy, the leading part played by our country among the great countries of the world; his words gave clear indication that he fully intends, in spite of present difficulties, to hold back the threat of inflation.
He would have liked, as he said himself, and I quote:
I need hardly say that as a new Minister of Finance I would have preferred the main features of my first Budget to be proposals to reduce taxation. But we can all take satisfaction from the fact that our problems are no longer the problems of overcoming slackness or stagnation but those of managing growth and prosperity. Our task is to sustain the longest economic expansion in Canadian history.
Those words, Mr. Speaker, show what a great Canadian he is, a Canadian who believes in the future of his country, a great Canadian who realizes that, even at the price of sacrifices, there is but one way to follow, which may not be the wide and easy way, the wide way of the easy life, but the more austere one, at least for the time being, of the

freely-accepted sacrifice for the well-being of everyone.
Perhaps the hon. members who spoke before me did not emphasize enough, in this budget debate, the remarkable character of what might be termed in sports a real performance. I am simply referring, sir, to the material aspect of the matter.
The Minister of Finance and his collaborators have in fact been working for months to prepare it, he had indicated his intention to present it to the house some time previously. He was ready on time.
He came here with a white paper, a document impressive by its contents as well as by its sincerity, and which, this year, achieved greater dimensions than usual. As customary, copies had been distributed in advance to the press and to leaders or financial critics of the various opposition parties. Moreover, all those documents had also been previously translated in the other language and similarly distributed.
Everything went off without a hitch, as it will be remembered, and it is certainly appropriate to congratulate-which is too seldom done perhaps-all those in the Finance Department, in the Bureau for Translations or elsewhere, who share in that annual operation. There, it seems to me, is an excellent example given to other government departments and more particularly to certain royal commissions which, at times, keep us waiting longer than we would wish for their reports.
There is another phenomenon which occurs every year and it is the foreseeable reaction of the leaders of the opposition parties. That is also part of the ritual.
Sometimes, one can guess or foresee the contents of the budget speech but one also goes wrong at times. On the other hand, it is seldom a mistake to say that whatever happens, opposition critics will never be satisfied. The short interviews they give newspapermen and radio and television reporters as they come out of the house could almost be written in advance. I do not think those should be taken seriously.
Today, they can complain of the deficit and say the government should do more to save the taxpayer's money but who does not recall the postwar years when the minister of finance of the time, Mr. Abbott, used to announce surpluses at times reaching hundreds of millions, but complaints were no fewer. It was said then that no government had the right to ask the taxpayer for one cent more than necessary.
April 19, 1966

This is not the case today, although the estimated deficit is relatively small compared to total expenditures. After all, an amount of $150 million out of more than $9 billion is an acceptable ratio. It is like borrowing 15 cents to buy something worth $9, when one does not have all the cash needed. Viewed from that angle, the deficit is more acceptable and shows how sound our economy is.
However, if the Minister of Finance had been perfectly free to do everything he wanted-I am thinking of the fixed expenditures he had to meet-I am sure he would have preferred to balance his budget, even announce a surplus which would have helped reduce the national debt.
Everybody becomes an economist the day after the budget is brought down.
Perhaps this was not the case a generation ago, because the influence the government could exercise on the economy was not known then. Things have changed a great deal today, and observing the country's economic situation, it is easy to imagine what one would have done under the circumstances as Minister of Finance. That is why I think the last budget speech did not really surprise anyone. The budget brought down on March 29 was, first of all, an extremely serious and reasonable budget.
Yet the minister was in a difficult situation. At the present time Canada is enjoying great prosperity. Generally speaking, practically every region is in full development. Except for some more or less chronically poverty-stricken areas-which are being looked after, as we know-there are no serious problems in any part of Canada. Unemployment is decreasing, and there is even concern, particularly in the larger cities, about a labour shortage, especially skilled labour.
Money circulates easily and cannot be said to be excessively concentrated in the hands of a few. The measures to stimulate the economy launched with the return to power of the Liberal party have been extremely successful, but at the same time have created problems of a different sort which are just as difficult to solve.
The climate of confidence prevailing in our country gave rise, to use the expression of Claude Ryan in he Devoir, to a thirst for investment. Understandably, under these conditions, with money rolling and investment opportunities multiplying constantly, the demand for consumer goods-for, in the final analysis, the consumer is the one who benefits from this state of affairs-is very
The Budget-Mr. Rochon great, greater than necessary for a sound national economy.
In saying this, Mr. Speaker, I am not telling anyone anything new. We can all see the rising cost of living. I spoke earlier of buying something for $9. While saying that I was trying to think of something one could buy today for $9.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
What amount of groceries does this represent in the local supermarket? Not much. Can clothing for a child be bought for this sum? Perhaps a pair of shoes? But when one has several children, or even just two or three, the money does not stretch very far. In 1910, a young civil servant could live on $600 a year. Today, he begins with a salary seven or eight times higher and he may not live any better, taking into account, of course, the change of circumstances since that distant period, although basically statistics indicate that since the end of World War II the average salary of the workman, for example, has increased more than the cost of living, which proves that the workman does live noticeably better now than he did then.
But this situation will not last forever and if the present trend continues all these advantages may be lost.
This was well understood by the Minister of Finance. This was certainly what the population understood also. In spite of the recriminations of the opposition, it can be said that the budget was well received. I was saying that the day following the budget everyone becomes somewhat of an economist; the average Canadian has perfectly understood this very simple principle that the pressure on prices cannot decrease as long as the amount of money in the hands of the consumers increases constantly. To reduce demand by increasing taxes is to avoid the risk of inflation.
But there is something of an alarming nature and somewhat of a paradox in that. It would be inhuman, in certain cases, to reduce the purchasing power of the taxpayer at a time when the cost of living increases rapidly. "The certain cases" to whom I am referring are the small taxpayers. It is in that light that the serious and complicated document which is the minister's budget speech takes a really human aspect because although it provides for a general increase in personal income tax, it grants the small wage earners real relief.
April 19, 196$

The Budget-Mr. Rochon
That is where some reservations could be made. It would be impossible to blame the minister for relieving the small taxpayer who has much more difficulty in finding $100 than the big taxpayer in finding $1,000 to pay his income tax.
I wonder, however, if the minister went far enough in that direction. The maximum amount in that respect is $5,000. Over that amount there is an income tax increase. But, in 1966, even $5,000 is not such a high income. Personally, I think that the minister might have been a little more generous and set at $7,000 the amount over which income tax would have gone up. It would have shown a more realistic view of things, for instance, the price of groceries or children's shoes, about which I spoke a little earlier.
Of course, it would have been necessary in that case to find the money elsewhere or to agree to a higher deficit. The easiest solution would have been, of course, to increase even more the income tax at higher levels. However, I think that would not have been a very good idea. Canadians are now among the most highly taxed people in the world -which is not so hard to understand in a wealthy country like ours-and when getting the money where it is-to speak like some socialists-we must be careful not to kill the goose that lays the golden eggs. An income of $12,000 a year does not allow anyone to live ostentatiously and, in spite of that, the state now claims almost $1,000, that is what it would cost one annually for instance to change one's car. It is quite enough.
Then where can we find the money needed to protect the economy while not increasing too much the already heavy burdens which the taxpayers have to bear? I admit that the answer is not easy to find and that, had I been the Minister of Finance, it is quite likely that I would have done the same thing.
However, while studying the rest of the budget and particularly the refundable tax of 10 per cent on gross profits which will from now on be imposed on corporations, I was reminded that during the war the government of the day whose minister of finance was Mr. Ilsley, adopted a similar policy with regard to the individual taxpayers. At that time, if I am not mistaken, it was called compulsory savings. I wonder if a similar method could not have been used, in spite of the administrative difficulties involved. And so, two birds could have been killed with one stone: decrease the amount of money in

circulation, and therefore the demand, without totally depriving the taxpayer of the enjoyment of his money.
There is an idea; it may not be of the brightest, but I wonder if the advisers to the Minister of Finance might not consider it.
The debate on the budget usually gives the opportunity to discuss matters that, in fact, have no direct bearing on it. Members are allowed to introduce local problems that are of particular interest to their ridings. That is why, without taking up too much of the time of the house, and after expressing in general terms what I thought of the seriousness of the speech made by the Minister of Finance, of the wisdom with which he intends to achieve the goal toward which every Canadian should aim: "stop the advance of inflation without making anyone suffer too much," that is why I should like to point out two matters of interest to the riding of Laval I represent here. For many years now, my predecessors and myself have asked for the dredging of the two rivers des Mille-lles and des Prairies which completely surround lle-Jesus, which became last fall the city of Laval, the second largest and most populated city in the province of Quebec, larger and more populated with its 185,000 inhabitants than the capital of the province, Quebec City.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to point out once more what this work would mean to our region in economic benefits. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) has understood it so well is so well aware of it, that he said last month, at Ste Rose where he addressed the Thousand Islands Yacht Club, while he was not speaking in an official capacity, that he understood and suggested, as a member of the executive committee, the importance of this work to a city in full progress that will become one of the most beautiful and modern cities of Canada, as can be foreseen from the architects' and town planners' overall plans. These words were from an authority and I wanted to remind you of them, Mr. Speaker. During the discussion of the estimates, I will go further into the idea of the Minister of Transport and I will submit in detail the reports of the government's engineers, those of public works as well as those of transport, who recommend the carrying out of those works for the economic development of the area as well as that of the Montreal region, since a report of the consulting engineers shows that the dredging of the two rivers and the building of dams would raise
April 19, 1966

the water level in the harbour of Montreal of approximately five feet.
The other matter deals with penitentiary employees, especially the clerks who could be better treated than they are presently. I studied the matter and I know it well since one of the largest penitentiaries of Canada, St. Vincent de Paul, is in my riding of Laval. During discussion of the Solicitor General's estimates, it will show you, Mr. Speaker, that a clerk P-A-5 receives only $4,800 while a grade 2 employee, which is the equivalent of a clerk P-A-5, gets $5,300; that a clerk P-A-3 receives only $4,380 while a guard of comparative grade gets $4,900.
As I say, I shall have the opportunity to come back to it, but in the meantime, I wanted simply to substantiate the claims of this class of employees who are as much in danger as their colleagues, the guards, since in their employment contract they are included in what is called the "reserve". In the case of a riot or any other trouble, they are called on the front line.
In closing, may I say that I am satisfied, as we all are on the government benches, that this year's budget will yield the anticipated results. If the minister succeeds, as he proposes to do, in stabilizing prices while safeguarding the prosperity we now enjoy, he will have deserved well of his country.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate tonight I propose to confine my remarks to one aspect only of the Budget, and that is the matter of dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements. In this connection I want to deal specifically with my own province of Prince Edward Island and try to present to this house as succinctly and as clearly as I can the particular plight of our province and why I think it should receive special recognition in the matter of fiscal assistance from the central government here in Ottawa.
I know-and the figures and statistics that I shall quote later will substantiate my contention-that our province, in its attempt to maintain for its citizens the same sort of provincial and municipal services that Canadians generally enjoy, is confronted with greater difficulties in public finance than any other province in Canada. We must, however, provide our people with the same standards of services that are being enjoyed by people living in other parts of Canada, and we must never forget that a Canadian citizen has certain inalienable rights whether he lives in
The Budget-Mr. McQuaid Prince Edward Island, Ontario or British
Columbia; and there can be no justification for having high standards of education, health, welfare and all the well-established functions of government in one part of Canada and pitiably low standards in another. We must deal with the needs of Canadian citizens wherever they may reside, and the federal government must arrive at financial arrangements which will enable each province to furnish to its people a reasonable standard of essential services.
National consideration must therefore be given to the needs of all partners in this great union. The growth and the economic problems of the province of Prince Edward Island must be the concern of every province in Canada. That is why I make this special appeal to the federal government tonight for special recognition in helping us solve these problems. We have strained our resources to the limit, Mr. Speaker, in an attempt to maintain our essential public services at a reasonable level, but we are still not able to establish and maintain national standards because of our inability to raise sufficient revenues from the sources of revenue at our disposal.
Why are these sources of revenue not available to us? They are not available to us for two reasons; first because of our small population, and second because of our low per capita income. Unfortunately, through no fault of our own, we are one of the provinces which has failed to grow in population over the years. We are now only 108,000 people, and since 1951 we have gained only 10 per cent in population. Compare this with the other provinces of Canada. Over that same 15-year period from 1951 to 1965, while we have gained only 10 per cent in population the provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta have gone up 50 per cent, the Provinces of Quebec and Newfoundland have gone up 40 per cent, and Manitoba, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have gone up 20 per cent.
Unfortunately, too, our young people are leaving our province in increasing numbers because central Canada affords brighter prospects and opportunities. With their departure the province loses not only the most efficient type of worker but also the progressive ability important to further expansion of industry and enterprise. Unfortunately only the very young and the very old stay with us and, as the Special Senate Committee on Aging

43 per cent; New Brunswick's revenue went up 44 per cent and its expenditures by only 34 per cent.
How long, I wonder, can that situation continue? How long can we continue to allow expenditures to exceed revenues by such large amounts and at the same time hope to maintain a solvent position? Our people have a deep respect for financial integrity and have demanded in the past that government spending be as commensurate as possible with ability to repay. For this reason successive governments have practised drastic economy in expenditures and have exploited every feasible means of raising provincial revenues. The province has tried to perform its functions with great frugality and economy but there are certain basic essentials which must be provided, and even when these are kept at the lowest possible level they are still high in relation to our small population and low tax potential; consequently the province has been going steadily behind each year.
The net increase in provincial debt for the year ending March 31, 1966, was $6 million, and as of March 31, 1965, the province had a net debt of $44 million plus an indirect debt of $14 million. This, Mr. Speaker, makes a total direct and indirect debt of $58 million, which is not very large when compared with the debt of many of the larger provinces, but when we consider it represents a per capita debt of $537 and that in our province we have not behind the debt the natural resources which are enjoyed by many of the other provinces of Canada, it is very large indeed. From March 31, 1958, to March 31, 1966, for example, revenues including what we received from Ottawa increased from $9,400,000 to $23 million, or almost 150 per cent, while expenditures during the same period increased from $10,800,000 to $30 million, or almost 215 per cent.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
These mounting deficits, Mr. Speaker, cannot continue indefinitely, and yet on what is the province able to cut back? Every item of expenditure in the provincial budget can be justified. Even then, our expenditures on essential services are below the standards enjoyed by people in the other provinces of Canada. Let us consider for example the field of education. In 1964, 24 per cent of our provincial revenue was applied to education as against the Canadian average of 30.9 per cent. We are the second lowest province in
April 19, 1966	COMMONS
Canada with regard to expenditures on education. The average salary of our teachers is only $2,783, the lowest in Canada. In Ontario, for example, the average salary of a teacher is $4,922; in Newfoundland, it is $2,818; in Nova Scotia, $3,504, and in New Brunswick, $3,254.
We have only 124 teachers in our schools today with university degrees. This is the lowest figure in Canada-11 per cent as compared to the Canadian average of 30.4 per cent of teachers with university degrees. We have only one with a doctorate, six with masters, and 117 with bachelor degrees. Teachers are just not remaining in the teaching profession in Prince Edward Island. We have only 75 teachers with 26 years or more experience; 145 with 16 to 25 years experience; 180 with 10 to 15 years experience and 245 with 4 to 9 years experience. Teachers require more advanced training in order to cope with a more advanced curriculum and they consequently, and rightly so, require more pay. Specialization in the teaching profession has become necessary and the small school, staffed with one or two teachers instructing in all subjects, can no longer furnish a sound, basic education for our students. We must not and we will not cut back expenditures on education, thereby neglecting the educational needs of our children. They must have available to them the best educational opportunities that are possible, because this will equip them with the means of making a better living.
An average male, for example, who goes only to grade eight in school will earn in later life an income of $3,526. If he completes high school he will earn $5,493 and if he gets a university degree he will earn $9,188. Can we be expected, therefore, to cut back our expenditure on education to the very definite detriment of our children? I say emphatically no, we cannot and we must not. Our children must have available to them the best educational opportunities that are possible. Equal educational opportunities should be available to all Canadians regardless of the economic circumstances of their province.
The government of our province is attempting to carry out a program of industrial development. However, Mr. Speaker, it has been said very correctly that industry cannot operate or expand in a vacuum. In order to flourish, it requires a friendly climate, one created in part by a broad structure of provincial and municipal services including highways, electric power, hospitals, welfare
DEBATES	4021
The Budget-Mr. McQuaid services and many others. Our expenditures on these items are by no means exorbitant and annual appropriations for the departments of agriculture and fisheries are very moderate. In short, Mr. Speaker, all costs are kept at the barest minimum level and as a result there are certain almost basic essentials which our province is not able to provide for its people, although they are entitled to them and they are being enjoyed by people living in other provinces of Canada.
As I mentioned previously, we have strained our resources to the limit in an attempt to maintain our essential public services at a reasonable level, but we are still not able to establish and maintain national standards. We are, as partners in this great confederation, entitled to enjoy these national standards. Since, through no fault of our own, we are not able to raise the money to provide them, we must receive federal assistance over and above the amounts which we are now receiving. In other words, we must receive a greater share of the taxes which are being paid to the federal government and this should come to us in the form of a special adjustment grant based on fiscal need.
In asking for this, Mr. Speaker, we are only asking for part of what is our own. Let us not forget that the federal tax revenues are the result of the collective effort of all our people. Merely because taxes are paid in one province does not mean that this revenue is necessarily produced in that province. Corporations and individuals in the central provinces, who pay taxes to the federal treasury, in many cases earn their incomes from businesses carried on in all the provinces of Canada.
We in Prince Edward Island have seen other provinces grow richer at our expense. We see every day the best of our youth being attracted to other provinces just as they are entering the period when they might become an asset to us. You will find in almost every part of Canada a great number of persons, born and educated in Prince Edward Island at our expense, who are now holding positions of trust and responsibility in the professional, academic, commercial and industrial fields and contributing by way of taxes to the economic advancement of the province in which they live. We are more than happy that we have been able to make this contribution to the economy of other parts of Canada but we cannot really afford it.
April 19. 1966

The Budget-Mr. McQuaid
We argue most vehemently, therefore, that we are entitled as of right to a special adjustment grant, the amount of which must be arrived at on the basis of fiscal need and not on the basis of some over-all formula worked out for all the provinces of Canada. Any attempt to meet the needs of Prince Edward Island based on a formula of universal application is doomed to failure. I am convinced that no formula of general application can give realistic recognition to the special financial problems of our province with its relatively low natural resources, its small population and its low per capita income.
In asking for this special treatment, Mr. Speaker, we must not be looked upon as beggars or poor relations, but rather as Canadians who have made and will continue to make a contribution to the development of this great nation. I think it was the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) who said at one provincial premiers conference in 1960 that we must get away from the idea that the premiers of the provinces come to Ottawa like well dressed, respectable bandits, desirous of breaking into the treasury in spite of the Herculean efforts of the Minister of Finance to retain its pristine purity. As I say, we are entitled as of right to this special adjustment grant.
Ahead of us, Mr. Speaker, lie great and challenging opportunities, but if we are to make the most of them in Prince Edward Island it is essential that we achieve more equitable and satisfactory fiscal arrangements, based on the fundamental principle of fiscal need. This is a situation which demands immediate action so that the people of Prince Edward Island may enjoy the same standards of public service as are being enjoyed by people in other parts of Canada.
I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that our province will not be discriminated against by reason of the fact our people did not elect anybody on the government side of the house at the last election. Such a suggestion has already been thrown out to the people of Prince Edward Island by the leader of the Liberal party in that province. This is what he said just a few days ago, immediately after the provincial election was announced. He said that we must elect a Liberal government in Prince Edward Island because of the deteriorating liaison between the Shaw administration and the federal government at Ottawa, which can only be remedied by a change of government on the island. I hope,

Mr. Speaker, some responsible person on the front benches would deny this statement and assure this house and the people of Prince Edward Island we will not be discriminated against by reason of the fact we did not elect anybody on the government side at the November 8 election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the very outset of my participation to the debate on the budget brought down by the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), I wish to state that his budget disappointed everybody. It was disappointing, discouraging and disgusting. The Canadian people did not expect that type of budget at all, because during the electoral campaign, barely four and a half months ago, the government did not promise that kind of budget, which would literally ignore the old people and children of Canada, our education, and would even fail to present a concrete program for our war against poverty in Canada.
The budget is a disappointment to the whole population, to all classes of society. When one realizes, Mr. Speaker, what this budget means for instance to the small wage earner, worker or farmer-and their name is legion-one can see a taxpayer earning $3,000 a year, who paid $22 in federal income tax before this budget, now pay $20 a year-I am talking here of a married taxpayer, with two children eligible for family allowance that is $2 less per year.
And what of those, Mr. Speaker, who earn less than $3,000 a year, who will not benefit of any tax exemption, who will have to pay sales tax on all kinds of things, on clothes and everything else, sales tax here, manufacturers tax there, taxes here and there and everywhere.
We know they are legion those who still earn less than $3,000 a year. Not so long ago, a member for Montreal was telling me that there are still in his riding, thousands of workers who earn from $1,900 to $2,000 a year. And in a riding where human beings are human beings as everywhere else in Canada, will those people, those workers, have any tax exemptions? Absolutely not. Will they have increased family allowances for their children? No. Will they have higher old age pensions? No. And the Minister of Finance delights in a system of that kind, telling us that our people, our business men will have to put a brake on economic expansion in
April 19. 1966

Canada; that even the government will have to postpone construction of government buildings and that even the government will have to reduce the rate of growth in Canada.
And, Mr. Speaker, over and above this, we are told that these measures will facilitate borrowing in Europe, that provincial, municipal and federal governments will have easier access to foreign capital as a result of the cancellation of the 15 per cent tax imposed on non-residents in Canada, on Canadian government bond interests. This exemption which came into effect on April 15, that is four days ago, is intended to facilitate the sale of debentures and bonds in the United States and Europe and to allow the three levels of government to get more easily the money required to pay the cost of public services.
In addition to public administrations, hospitals and educational institutions, which will have their bonds guaranteed by the provinces, will also have the same type of exemptions.
The Minister of Finance stated in his budget speech that he does not want to make decisions in this connection on corporate or personal loans before the general revision of the Income Tax Act which will be dealt with in the report of the Carter commission on taxation.
Mr. Speaker, those are points raised by the Minister of Finance in his budget speech.
The government, of which the Minister of Finance is a member, during the election, promised to increase old age pensions. We expected that the government or the Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, would announce an increase to $100 per month in pensions paid to our people aged 60 or over. Nothing doing. They turn a deaf ear when it comes to raising pensions.
As far as family allowances are concerned, the minister knows that they have not changed since 1945, and he also knows that the cost of living has at least tripled in that period of 21 years.
What do the minister and the government do to increase old age pensions according to the cost of living index. Nothing at all. And the government boasts on the hustings that it wages a war against poverty in Canada.
Through its recent budget, the government creates new indigents in Canada and lets poverty work havoc all over our confederation, all over Canada.
Mr. Speaker, by this system, we are now taxing taxes and nobody protests against that.

The Budget-Mr. Caouette As concerns automobiles, the government takes right away $600 on a $3500 car, which means that the automobile would cost only $2900 without the federal tax.
Not only is a $600 tax levied on a $3500 automobile but provinces are allowed to levy a tax; for instance, the province of Quebec levies a provincial tax of 6 per cent on the federal tax of $600 on a car. This means that in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, and also in other provinces, we pay $36 as provincial tax on the federal tax, and the federal government says nothing. The provincial government is happy to take its $36.
Nothing is being done to change this system. The Minister of Finance is aware of it. Instead of getting at the financial system, the minister says: stop the economic expansion, stop building air terminals, roads, and developing your country, stop that expansion which could be detrimental to the future of Canada.
Instead of putting forward a program intended to stop or restrict the economic expansion of Canada, the minister should have established clearly a means of distributing our Canadian affluence. The minister knows that affluence does exist in our stores. He knows that our farmers can produce more, and that our manufacturers can manufacture more. The minister knows that production renews itself and increases from year to year and that stocks of previous years are not consumed, so that we are confronted today with the following situation: our stores, our businessmen, our industrialists in their buildings, in their storerooms, on their shelves, have all kinds of products in such quantities that our consumers are not able to consume what is actually for sale in Canada.
Instead of offering a system by which the Canadian taxpayers could go and draw on their own wealth and resources, on their tremendous production, the minister tells us: "Stop growing, stop developing, stop!" What will the minister say when industry, for example, is confronted with automation?
Does the minister wish to ask me a question?

election, Mr. Lesage's government was borrowing $100 million from British Columbia. Not too bad for a bankrupt government.

The hon. member for Saint-Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) is smiling; he will be helping his co-religionists of the province of Quebec on June 5. Why does he always put the touch on the builders of the country and not on those who are gobbling it up?
I mentioned that the age of automation is coming and that the department will be hard put to find an appropriate administration, a financial administration conscious of the realities in Canada.

This means, Mr. Speaker, that in the south of the United States, in California and elsewhere in Canada, people are beginning to realize the logic of the national dividend advocated by Major Douglas, to fight against poverty efficiently in any country of the world. Against these solutions which would efficiently combat poverty, the fact is brought forward that a number of economists are not in agreement over the Social Credit propositions. In Quebec, we have economists who believe in Social Credit. Here are some of them: Mr. Yordan Kostakeff, professor of economics; Mr. Ernest Gregoire who was for 35 years professor of economics at Laval University, Ernest Gregoire, a former mayor of Quebec City; Mr. Robert Theobald, who accepts the principles of Social Credit, as well as Mr. John Snyder, who advocates the distribution to the consumers of wealth and plenty.
These people agree that the Creditist proposals should be tried instead of criticized. Instead of ridiculing the creditist proposals, let us try to put them into practice in Canada; then we will no longer have to read budget speeches such as that of the Minister of Finance the other day in which he announced unprecedented prosperity in Canada: a prosperity illustrated by the dissatisfaction of all the classes of society.
In fact we are witnessing ever-increasing strikes, not only in Quebec but in all of Canada: strikes of teachers, of students, of Canadian mailmen, of Hydro-Quebec engineers, of truckers in Ontario, of farmers in northern Quebec and in the Lake St. John region technicians strike.

But even if a workman were to earn $10 an hour, if he must pay $350 for a suit, $200 for rent, if in fact he pays three times what the goods are worth, where will he be? Exactly where he was before. tMr. Caouette.]
riches, wealth and production of the country according to the work of Canadians.

That is the solution which would end fights between management and labour, and which would remove this general dissatisfaction within the whole population, not only in labour and farming, but in the small local businesses, in industry which faces unsold production, and in all social classes affected. The Minister of Finance knows too well-he knows it as well as I do-that the financial system is not adapted to Canadian needs.
The other day I reread the speech made by my colleague for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), who said: "Why is it that the United States government succeeds in creating finance? Why is it that we, Canadians, have to borrow on the United States market to develop our national heritage? If we have the brains, the labour and the physical capabilities of building public hospitals and buildings, not only in Ottawa, but also in Hull, of building schools in Canada, in short, if we have all the physical potential, with greater reason we should use the Bank of Canada to finance everything the Canadian people are capable of developing and building in this country.

We have huge quantities of minerals: copper mines, gold mines, iron mines, but we must ask the Americans permission to develop this tremendous wealth.
Mr. Speaker, this budget is a sucker offered to the Canadian people: a tax increase. The budget tells the Canadian people exactly the opposite of what the government promised before November 8, 1965. The government
April 19. 1966

can make promises but it is unable to keep them after the election. We should have benefited from tax reductions instead of being loaded with tax increases. And it is clearly stated here that six out of ten taxpayers will be paying more taxes, possibly up to 14 per cent more.

GRAIN-TROIS-RIVlfiRES-POSSIBLE CLOSING OF ELEVATORS

Mr. Speaker, the other day I put a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) in which I asked him, in effect, if he would consider taking urgent action to cope with the serious crisis facing the grain elevators of Trois-Rivieres.
I have brought up the matter on two or three occasions, but any action seems to lag alarmingly. This is constructive criticism and 1 have no intention of blaming anyone. However, no solution seems to be forthcoming and no thought given to repercussions which are naturally detrimental to the economy of the St. Maurice region of the province and even to the national economy. The grain elevators of Trois-Rivieres handle wheat from the west. This is known to be very important to the economy of the country. They handle great amounts of it, as may be seen in the report of the National Harbours Board which we were given today. In fact, for last year only, the total amount of merchandise handled at the Trois-Rivieres wharf was about 5,222,689 tons. The report further asys that grain exports are still increasing.
I think that if a solution to the problem is not found soon the grain elevators will have to close.
What is the problem? I shall state it briefly. Until now, the grain elevators paid some $26,000 a year in taxes to the municipalities; suddenly, they were required to pay some $280,000, an increase of over 1000 per cent.


You will understand that this is prohibitive, seeing that the Canadian Wheat Board fixes the handling charges and that our grain elevators compete with others which are not so burdened.
The only way we can solve this problem is to bring together all the people concerned, namely, the National Harbours Board, the operators of harbour facilities, the municipal council of Trois-Rivieres, and in all probability, the Municipal Board of the Quebec legislature, as well, because everyone will have to contribute his share in order to find a solution, which would probably be spread out over a period of three, four or five years.
Grain elevators directly provide a living to some 300 to 350 people as well as to the handlers who live in the neighbourhood; in turn, these people provide a living for corollary or subsidiary industries, namely trucking and other such industries.
Under the circumstances, owing to the vast industrial development which is going to take place in the Trois-Rivieres area, should these facilities be denied to the area, I think it would be a real disaster for all the Mauricie, which includes, by the way, Champlain county, Saint-Maurice-Lafleche county, part of Maskinonge county as well as Nicolet county, and of course, the county of Trois-Rivieres.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the hon. Minister of Transport, taking into account precisely all the possible consequences of such a crisis upon regional, provincial and national economies, to lead the way in order to hasten this procedure, this settlement, this solution.
I know that the municipality of Trois-Rivieres is concerned. I know that something has been done already. Mr. George Lloyd, of the National Harbours Board, already went on the site to discuss the question, but the proposed solution does not seem acceptable as such and no conclusion has been reached anyway. I know that he is supposed to go back there soon.
I suggest that the hon. Minister of Transport and the National Harbours Board had better give Mr. George Lloyd a free hand, so to speak, so that he may find a solution before it is too late.
With the most constructive possible intent, I should like to appeal to the minister most insistently, and I know that in so doing I
April 19, 1966

reflect the wishes of all those concerned in my constituency. Thus will we prevent a very acute crisis.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister without Portfolio):
speechtext:
With your leave, Mr. Speaker, I shall reply on behalf of the Minister of Transport.
The problem of the grain elevator company at Trois-Rivieres referred to by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres arises solely from the expiry in 1964 of a tax agreement between the elevator company and the city. In 1965, the city fully assessed the elevator company and this resulted in a greatly increased tax bill for 1965. I understand that the elevator company has instituted legal action to set aside the increased assessment.
Despite the fact that the cost increase to the elevator company at Trois-Rivieres is not due to any action of the National Harbours Board, that board, in co-operation with the city of Trois-Rivieres and the Trois-Rivieres Chamber of Commerce, is attempting to work out arrangements which will lessen the impact of municipal taxes on the principal users of the harbour.
These arrangements require not only action by the board, as suggested by the hon. member for Trois-Rivieres but also concurrent action by the city. I can certainly assure the hon. member that the National Harbours Board has shown its willingness to co-operate to the extent of its ability to do so, but it would not seem appropriate for me to give the impression of interfering in municipal matters at Trois-Rivieres such as the tax relations between the city and a private company.
The hon. member asked whether the minister was willing to appoint a special committee to look into the matter at once with the interested parties. This would not seem to be necessary, because in fact, though not in name, such a special committee already exists by virtue of the fact that representatives of the city, the elevator company and the National Harbours Board are discussing the matter extensively.
I hope that the matter will be brought to a successful conclusion.

speechtext:
I asked a question the other day concerning the reference in the budget address of the Minister of

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Finance (Mr. Sharp) to the deferment of construction of the Northumberland causeway. It is clear to anyone who is familiar with the maritime provinces and their economy that transportation has been and is a major and most important issue in that area. Communications with the mainland have been of the essence of the social and economic life of Prince Edward Island since the time of confederation. One can say without hesitation that the provision of adequate communications with the mainland is a federal obligation. It is therefore incumbent on those of us who represent the province to remind constantly those in charge of the national administration of their obligation in this respect.
The causeway project, one which was long sought and one which has transcended partisanship in our province and beyond it, activates us all. It was therefore with profound disappointment, shock and surprise that I listened to the Minister of Finance the other night while he outlined his restrain-the-boom technique, with particular reference to our long sought and desperately needed transportation project.
There has been a great deal of discussion, and my question was motivated by concern about the semantic exercises which have been carried on as to whether or not a rescheduling meant, or means, a deferment. I can only form my judgment, as is fair and proper, on the basis of the utterances of the minister himself.
One of the most important sections in the budget address spoke of the necessity for the government to review its construction program and defer a number of projects, as can be found in Hansard at page 3381.

speechtext:
The suggestion is to defer or reschedule a number of specific projects. Now rescheduling is apparently not a deferment. Yet I find that after the minister listed the five projects concerned be said:
I regret and I am sure everyone in this house regrets, that it is necessary to defer these projects-

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
And among the five projects are a grain elevator at Prince Rupert-the problem there was that the tenders were too high-the proposed new taxation building in Ottawa and a national museum, some less urgent work at airports, some harbour and marine works in coastal areas where there is serious pressure on the construction industry and, last, some smaller public buildings in Ontario and British Columbia.
Among this interesting collection of projects is the great Northumberland causeway under class "d". Why? It is to minimize the pressures on the peak summertime employment market, and maximize winter employment possibilities. I would be interested to know where that minister, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mcllraith), or any other minister finds these dreadful and overpowering pressures upon our labour force. If he would consult the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) he would find the last report indicates that the Atlantic province unemployment figure stands at 10.5, a drop from 10.9.
I would be interested to know when any project need be deferred because of lack of available labour. If it is not a shortage of labour, it is also not because we are galloping into excessive prosperity in the Atlantic region. Any minister need only read the second report of the Economic Council to find there a prescription not of restraint but of what our region needs in acceleration.
For the government on one hand to seek to encourage industry to move in and assist the economy of the region, and then exercise unnecessary and unwarranted restraint in one of its projects, leads me to believe that the reasons are not economic but political.
I quote from the Charlottetown Guardian of November 10, 1965, these words in its editorial notes:
"We spent $100,000,000 in Prince Edward Island and we didn't get a seat there" complains revenue minister E. S. Benson. It was asinine misstatements of this kind that helped them lose the two seats they had.
I hate to believe that it is for political considerations. I hate to believe that it is a five cent speech, Mackenzie King theory, once again being resurrected, but I would like very much to find an economic reason and I have not yet been able to do so in all the post-dated explanations and equivocations. I would simply ask the government to admit it


made a mistake in including this project, and that it push forward with an essential development in our area to help the economy of the Atlantic provinces, rather than hinder it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hasten to assure the hon. member that the Northumberland strait causeway is not being delayed in any way. The completion date is unchanged. It remains as it was when stated in the first announcement. What has been done here-and this fact has been asserted in a press release from myself, in correspondence from the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Pearson) and in other statements-is that a certain rescheduling has been made since the preliminary statement.
The rescheduling has only to do with the time of the maximum workload in the area. This is being done for the benefit of the maritime provinces, in particular for the wonderful province from which the hon. member comes.
As a result of this new timetable we are assured of a significant volume of winter work in late 1966 and early 1967, which is exactly the time of year that the hon. member has complained about when giving statistics on winter unemployment. This work activity will come at a time of the year when work is normally needed in the hon. member's province. It will be a positive factor in the economy of the province.
The new schedule provides for uninterrupted efforts to build the P.E.I. approach to the proposed nine mile crossing. Tenders for the 41 mile approach road will be called in June, following completion of land acquisition.
This road, at the P.E.I. end of the crossing, will be completed in the latter part of 1967 as a step toward the construction of the main structure and it will serve as a hauling route for the project. Plans for the two mile New Brunswick approach causeway will be completed in July, with the call for tenders expected in August. This will permit the contractor to be on the site for work throughout the coming winter period. Of course, there is no alteration in the existing schedule for the approach road begun last year and it is moving ahead on schedule, to be completed by August of this year. This is perhaps a little better than on schedule.
